subtopic: POWERS OF BOARD RESPECTING THE MARKETING OF WHEAT-INITIAL PAYMENT OF 70 CENTS A BUSHEL

speechtext: Hon. W. D. EULER (Minister of Trade and Commerce) moved the third reading of Bill No. 63, to amend the Canadian Wheat Board Act, 1935.

subtopic: POWERS OF BOARD RESPECTING THE MARKETING OF WHEAT-INITIAL PAYMENT OF 70 CENTS A BUSHEL
speechtext:
In the past few days we have listened to a number of speeches on this question, ranging all the way from sincere endeavours to show the need in Canada for a higher price than this bill proposes, to the exhibition of active buffoonery to which we were treated yesterday by the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot). I refer to his speech in these terms because I am sure he realizes quite well that it is absurd to suggest that men who have lived in western Canada for many years, whether they be farmers or school teachers, men who have lived in the rural districts and listened day after day to discussions on matters of farming, are not fully informed as to the trials and tribulations of the people of the west
and well qualified to speak on matters relating to the farming industry. Personally I have been a farmer in the west since 1909, and I think I am as well qualified as any hon. member to speak on this question.
Up to the present we have stressed two main points: first, the need of higher prices to make it possible for farmers to continue in operation; second, the justification for the farmers making this demand.
Going back a few years, we remember that by 1928, generally speaking, conditions in western Canada were fairly satisfactory. At that time the farmers had assumed pretty heavy responsibilities, and in large measure on account of their realization that low prices would return, and the endeavour on their part to place themselves in a position to stand up against such unfavourable conditions. They therefore took steps to increase their holdings of land and to acquire the more modern machinery which would make it possible for them to farm these lands efficiently.
In 1930 prices crashed to a level lower than had been known, with but few exceptions, during the preceding three hundred years, and these low prices were followed by five or six, and in some districts by seven or eight, years of drought. Farmers who by 1928 had built up strong reserves in the bank, and in some cases held ten or fifteen thousand dollars' worth of life insurance, saw their savings wiped out and were forced to take the cash surrender value of their insurance. In many cases the machinery they had acquired was not paid for. In a great many cases their land was being purchased under a crop agreement. It was only natural that after five or six years of these conditions the farmers found themselves in a hopeless state. Many of them in good faith invoked the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, hoping thereby to be able to meet their obligations. But as we all know, the farmers who prior to 1936 went under that act did not receive as sympathetic consideration as the farmers who have gone under it since that time. They signed agreements which it has been impossible for them to fulfil. I hope it may be possible to have these cases reopened; otherwise it is only a question of time when those who went under the act prior to 1936 will lose their land.
The reason we are urging that the price be raised above 70 cents is that farmers who have gone through the long period of drought and low prices have had their reserves wiped out, and it is very necessary that they should be allowed a breathing spell, largely to enable them to regain their poise. Some people may
Canadian Wheat Board

point out that the price proposed involves a reduction of only ten cents, but remember that the price was held at 90 cents, so that in reality the reduction represents twenty cents a bushel. I would urge the government, even at this late day, to reconsider their action and allow the price to remain at 80 cents. I emphasize the fact that the Bracken conference, which truly represents western Canada and which made a thorough investigation of the whole question, while realizing that 80 cents will not provide a solution of the difficulty, urge that the price be maintained at 80 cents for at least another year in order to give the farmers a chance to get back on their feet and to carry on, which they will not be able to do if the amount is only 70 cents.
It has been urged that bill 83 will more than compensate the farmer for any loss he may incur through the reduction of price from 80 to 70 cents. But as we have pointed out, bill 83 will bring about a slight increase of cost to all farmers and will benefit only very few; in some years it may not benefit any.
While on this subject I should like to deal briefly with the position of the drought areas- because in my opinion bill 83 is more a form of drought relief than a crop insurance measure. It must be remembered that to-day the existence of the drought area is recognized as the result of a mistake in federal policy, and for that reason it must be regarded as to a large extent a federal liability. That measure will provide only a limited amount of protection for farmers in the drought area, so that it cannot be fairly considered as in any shape or form compensating the farmers in the other rural districts of the west for any reduction of price.
The hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Ross) said he thought it was a mistake to refer to cost of production per bushel; that we should speak of cost on an acreage basis. But it must be realized that costs on an acreage basis also vary considerably. In a wet year the weed growth is considerably greater than it is in a dry year and therefore the cost of handling summer-fallow in a wet year will be greater than the cost in a dry year. In certain areas where the land is very weedy the cost of summer-fallowing will be greater than the cost of handling clean summer-fallow. If you are going to stubble in it is cheaper to stubble in a crop than to summer-fallow, and in some years a stubble crop will give as good a return as a summer-fallow crop. It is therefore extremely difficult to say what the cost will be. We have not suggested that you can determine what the rMr. Quelch.]
cost of production is, but it seems only logical to take the average yield in the west over a period of years. The minister, I believe, said that in Saskatchewan the average yield was 13 bushels to the acre or thereabouts, and in Alberta it is in the neighbourhood of 16 bushels over a period of years. Taking the average of these two we get a yield of 14| bushels to the acre, and, dividing the average cost by the average yield, we get approximately the average cost per bushel, which, I presume, should give an idea of what the price ought to be to make it possible for the majority of the farmers to carry on.
I quite realize that in a drought area the farmers would have to have perhaps $5 or $6 a bushel to make it possible to continue on that basis, but it is impossible to establish crop insurance on an actuarial basis in such an area. The fact is that a large number of areas will have to go out of production so far as grain farming is concerned, and the sooner that is brought about, the better. Such areas will eventually go back to grazing. I submit, therefore, that to try to introduce a scheme that will make it possible for drought areas to continue in the grain farming business is a mistaken policy. Our objective in that direction must be to find ways and means of taking these areas out of grain production, and that would bring about a reduction in the cost of production on the average throughout western Canada. And if we must compete in the world's market, as apparently we have to, then the lower we can bring the average cost of production the better it will be if we are to make it possible for the western farmer to dispose of his grain in the world market to a greater extent than at the present time. I maintain, therefore, that it is a mistake to try to bring drought areas into this question at all. We should recognize that it is an entirely different problem, the result of a mistaken federal policy, and therefore we should concentrate on the problem of making it possible for the majority of farmers in western Canada, outside that area, to continue in the grain farming business.
I return to the Bracken conference. They took that point of view and their conclusion was that in order for the majority of farmers of western Canada to continue in business and to regain their feet, after the trials and tribulations they have been through during the last eight or nine years, it was necessary to guarantee a price of at least 80 cents. It is not a question whether that is the cost of production. I agree with the hon. member for Moose Jaw that it is not cost of production, but it is better than 70 cents and it would give the farmers a chance to build up

Canadian Wheat Board
reserves again. For western Canada cannot be on a safe footing until the farmers have built up reserves. Bill 83 will not make it possible to establish those reserves because it will deal only with certain farmers. There, will be many farmers with total crop failure who will not get any protection under bill 83. The only protection the farmer can hope to get in the last analysis is something that will enable him to build up a reserve so that when the bad years come he will have something to live on. In 1928 we had such reserves and for two or three years the farmers were able to live on them; but after five, six, seven and eight years of distress it is only natural that their reserves should have been wiped out entirely, so that to-day the farmer is operating on a shoestring. And so I again urge the government-

subtopic: POWERS OF BOARD RESPECTING THE MARKETING OF WHEAT-INITIAL PAYMENT OF 70 CENTS A BUSHEL
speechtext: Farming in eastern Canada, generally speaking, is entirely different from farming in the west. It is a different type of farming, which does not need as large a reserve to enable the farmer to operate as is needed in western Canada. Grain farming is altogether different from small stock farming.

subtopic: POWERS OF BOARD RESPECTING THE MARKETING OF WHEAT-INITIAL PAYMENT OF 70 CENTS A BUSHEL

subtopic: POWERS OF BOARD RESPECTING THE MARKETING OF WHEAT-INITIAL PAYMENT OF 70 CENTS A BUSHEL
speechtext:
Small stock farming is entirely different from grain farming. Any hon. member who is familiar with grain farming and who has also engaged in small mixed farming knows that the statement I make is sound, that the grain farmer must have a larger reserve behind him than the small stock farmer requires. In western Canada there are
many small stock farmers without reserves, but they have their weekly cream and poultry cheques coming in. The grain farmer may have a small poultry cheque coming in, but very often he has no cream cheques to depend upon. Moreover, cows in such an area would be a liability two years out of three. In a dry year the farmer need not worry about feeding his tractor; all he has to do is to find the fuel for it when in operation; but if he has animals he must find ways and means of keeping them alive during a drought. It is therefore nonsense to suggest that the western grain grower should go into mixed farming. In some areas, yes; but in other areas it would be suicidal, especially in the southern part, which is a straight wheat farming district. Nor would it do to suggest oats, barley or grass, because it is not a good grass country. As I say, it is straight wheat; and as the hon. member ifor Grey-Bruce (Miss Macphail) said, the worst thing that could happen to eastern Canada would be for the west to go out of grain and into mixed farming, because it would flood the east with various live stock products with the result that prices would crash.

subtopic: POWERS OF BOARD RESPECTING THE MARKETING OF WHEAT-INITIAL PAYMENT OF 70 CENTS A BUSHEL
speechtext: Do you think that the Ontario farmers have been having a prosperous time?

subtopic: POWERS OF BOARD RESPECTING THE MARKETING OF WHEAT-INITIAL PAYMENT OF 70 CENTS A BUSHEL
speechtext: No, but the mixed farmer can unquestionably carry on with a far smaller reserve than can the grain farmer of western Canada, because the grain farmer has to keep up machinery and he must have fuel, whereas the small live stock farmer needs but a very small amount of machinery. I have been in both businesses and I know what I am talking about, whereas the hon. member is not familiar with western conditions.

subtopic: POWERS OF BOARD RESPECTING THE MARKETING OF WHEAT-INITIAL PAYMENT OF 70 CENTS A BUSHEL
speechtext: And you are not familiar with conditions in Ontario.

subtopic: POWERS OF BOARD RESPECTING THE MARKETING OF WHEAT-INITIAL PAYMENT OF 70 CENTS A BUSHEL

On the question of justification, I do not want to go over the ground again because I have already discussed the subject from this point of view. But for a number of years western Canada has been contributing in the neighbourhood of $100,000,000 a year to eastern Canada, and that in itself is complete justification for western Canada demanding that a small portion of that contribution should be used as a fund to guarantee the farms in the west against destitution- and low prices will mean destitution. If the hon. member across the way will stop mumbling and wait until I am through to make any remarks he wants to make, I suggest it would facilitate the discussion.
Canadian Wheat Board

I admire very much the courage of hon. members opposite who rose to protest against the 70 cent price. It is not easy for members of the Liberal party to vote against the party, but the people of western Canada will rightly appreciate that sacrifice and the stand which those hon. gentlemen have taken. I was disappointed in the attitude of the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker). He suggested that it would be quite wrong to vote against this bill because it would defeat the government and we should lose all the legislation. That seems to me a puerile argument, scarcely one that this house should be expected to take seriously. The question before the house is whether or not we are willing to sabotage- again I use that term-agriculture in western Canada. That is what it means when you allow the price to fall to the level of 47 cents. Western Canada has every right and justification to be dissatisfied. It is not a question of pleading for relief; it is a question of demanding that which they have a right to demand, namely, a price of at least 80 cents a bushel.

Just one other point. I was endeavouring yesterday to get certain information. I said that if this bill had been brought down sooner and had gone to the special committee, we would have asked for certain information which I think is due to the country. Last night the argument was put up that we did not give it in 1935, that we got it only up to a certain period. I have here the evidence and the report of the special committee on the wheat board act of 1935.

Canadian Wheat Board
The sittings were mostly held in June. On June 27 we had the evidence of Mr. Findlay and Mr. Mclvor giving the standing of Mr. McFarland in his stabilization operations right up to the first of June, only one month before the bill passed the house. I was asking yesterday for information starting away back last August, September and October, and also with respect to last January. I just want to make it plain to the house that I was not asking for anything unreasonable but only for information similar to that which the opposition asked for in 1935, and which they got practically up to the date of the sittings. Here is the record to show that I am right.
I just want to make a final plea for the reinstatement of the advisory committee. subtopic: POWERS OF BOARD RESPECTING THE MARKETING OF WHEAT-INITIAL PAYMENT OF 70 CENTS A BUSHEL
speechtext:
I wish to occupy only a very few minutes on the third reading of this bill. I am not surprised at the acrobatic performances of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) and of hon. members opposite and of the members of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation in this house on this grain problem. Not by the widest stretch of the imagination can this bill be said to be a work for the general advantage of Canada. It is not a long-term policy. The price should be left until August or September, left to the wheat board and a capable administrator like Mr. McFarland. This bill is not in the interests of the prairie farmers. It would be far better and would cost far less money to adopt the suggestions made on second reading of the grain board bill in 1935, referred to by the very able member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley), who has given a great deal of study to the matter and much valuable information to the house on this question. It would be far better if the country would nationalize for a while the grain crop as an emergency measure-it would cost Canada millions less than these grain bills-and see that the middlemen are cut out altogether. Under this bill the middlemen will be still flourishing at the old stand. We should widen, not restrict, the wheat board and give them a free hand.
Various briefs were presented regarding this question before the Rowell commission by the three prairie provinces. What has become of those briefs? It was said in the debate on the address that we were to wait on this problem until the Rowell commission report was received. That report has not been received, yet we have these bills to forestall it. The industrial workers have to wait for the Rowell commission report; why should not the wheat board be allowed a free hand.
The hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Ross) said the six cent preference was of little value. I have a great deal of respect for him as an old friend, but I think he is all wrong on this bill. What good was the six cent preference, he said? The house has spent ten days discussing these bills but we have not had ten minutes' discussion on a much more important thing. The security of the country is better than opulence and Canada's export trade in wheat may be ruined by the dictators.
This bill limits the amount that can be sold to the board by one producer to 5,000 bushels, tying their hands, taking away their powers, and making the board nothing but a lot of office boys for the Minister of Agriculture. This bill will have the effect of providing relief for some and not for others. The country has lost the benefit of the Ottawa agreements six cent preference in the British market, and the United States have seized the opportunity and taken it from us. They are sending 100 million bushels of wheat to Britain for rubber and tin. All you are doing in these bills will amount to nothing in a world crisis and emergency in world affairs, because three or four submarines can sink your shipping in the seven seas and Britain will get none of our wheat at all and will be starved out by the submarine menace.
How do they treat the people who are going to contribute largely to this cost-the industrial workers? As I have said many times, I am not for east or west or north or south; I believe we should have a system of protection for all the people of Canada all of the time, and not for some of the people some of the time. The principle of this bill is to rob collective Peter to pay selective Paul. Yesterday when I was calling the attention of the house to the lot of a few industrial workers who cannot get bread or lodging, and have not six cents let alone seventy cents in their pockets, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) did nothing but turn it off on the provinces and municipalities to pay. Then when a big deputation of clergy complain in Toronto and go to the municipalities they are told to go and see the province and the dominion, and
Canadian Wheat Board

the Minister of Labour said it was the provinces' burden. What kind of protection is that-protection for one part of the country and not for another? The municipalities are made the goat of it all. The application of this six cent British preference has gone forever.
I may tell hon. members opposite that without the six cent preference they will never get back their markets abroad. Britain, you see, is now dealing with others. Why did not the minister lay on the table of the house all the correspondence for which I asked when this bill was in committee? I requested the correspondence with Hon. H. A. Wallace, Secretary for Agriculture at Washington, with regard to joint action between the two boards on the north American continent to handle the marketing of the wheat of Canada and the United States in an orderly way which would help us. Will the minister do something along these lines, in order that the people of these two countries may be sure of their right share of the markets of Europe in these times of emergency, and under present conditions in the grain trade?
We can blame hon. gentlemen opposite for the condition of the grain trade in Canada to-day. As I said before, for many years they have worn a coat of many colours in connection with this question. It was said last February the wheat board was to be abolished; then it was to be retained; then Canada was to get out of pegging. January, February, March and April went by; now it is May, but the various acrobatic performances of the Minister of Agriculture in connection with this question and all these bills have not surprised me, because hon. gentlemen opposite have been everything by fits and starts and nothing long on the grain business. We are told that the price of 70 cents is not enough. It should be only what the country's ability is to pay next August, and it should be left to the wheat board. The hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas) and the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) say 70 cents will reduce the people of the prairies to the level of serfs and to the conditions of European peasants. Let me tell them that the serfs are not all on the prairies; there are many of them walking the streets of the industrial cities to-day-fine industrial workers who get nothing; broken down men who have never been out of work before, many of them returned soldiers, without six cents let alone seventy cents in their pockets. But they have to suffer all this while they wait for the report of the Rowell commission, while others get all kinds of handouts. The wheat board and it alone should handle all these bills.

subtopic: POWERS OF BOARD RESPECTING THE MARKETING OF WHEAT-INITIAL PAYMENT OF 70 CENTS A BUSHEL
speechtext:
The other day the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Ross) stated that you could not form an estimate of the cost of producing a bushel of wheat. We are of the opinion that this bill does not cover the cost of production, and we consider that the western wheat industry should be given the same treatment that is given every other industry in Canada, especially in view of the fact that the western farmers have contributed so greatly to the prosperity and development of this country. Now that they are in danger of becoming bankrupt I think the question is most serious. The cost of production at least should be assured to those people.
The hon. member for Moose Jaw went on to say that while you could not fix the cost of producing a bushel of wheat you might be able to fix the cost per acre. We would have no objection to that. Just a moment ago the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) referred to the fact that an estimate could be made in regard to the cost per acre. I happen to have under my hand some figures I received from the bureau of statistics on January 26, 1939, indicating the enormous sums of money contributed to the wealth of this country by the farmers of the west and also giving average yields per acre over a ten year period. I have no objection to basing the cost of production on a ten-year average, but I have every objection to forming this estimate of cost in the manner indicated in a statement by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) some time ago. He told us on what the department based the estimate of 60 cents, and then for no good reason at all that figure was raised to 70 cents. This is what the minister said, and I am now referring to page 2617 of Hansard for April 5:
Mr. Johnston (Bow River):	How did the
government arrive at the 80 cent price?
Mr. Gardiner: That is the set price.
Mr. Johnston (Bow River): But what was the basis on which it was set?
Then follows the statement to which I should like to direct attention:
Mr. Gardiner: I shall deal with that later. It is a matter of opinion, largely.
In a matter so serious as this it is ridiculous that any capable government should even attempt to fix the cost of production as a matter of opinion or by a lot of guesswork. In this report which I received from the bureau of statistics last January I find that the average yield per acre for the province of Manitoba over a ten-year period was 13-84 bushels. Following up the suggestion of the hon. member for Moose Jaw, if you can form an estimate of producing an average acre of

Canadian Wheat Board
wheat and you know the average yield, surely you can get down to a reasonably sound figure as to the cost of producing a bushel of wheat. The figure I mentioned was for Manitoba. I could give the yearly average for that ten-year period from 1929 to 1938, of the farm value of these crops, which runs into millions of dollars. The drought area in the southern parts of the three western provinces should be considered as a national responsibility. Then the remainder of the provinces could be put quite nicely on an insurance plan. We have always contended that the provinces of the west should have a form of crop insurance but that the drought area should be taken out of those provinces and considered a national responsibility, because that drought area is caused by elements over which human beings have no control. That has always been considered a national responsibility and must continue to be so regarded in the future. For that reason I think it should be taken out of the rest of the western provinces, which could then come under a crop insurance plan. Then if you want to put on a one per cent tax I do not think there would be any great objection. The Searle letter continues:
Such a policy, of course, is excellent for the survival of Canadian tariff-protected manufacturing industry, but what, we venture to ask, about agriculture? And particularly what about the great western wheat industry under such a policy? For the ability of that wheat industry to compete (the tariffs now make production costs very high) in the most important markets it has, i.o. foreign markets, is to-day being most

seriously harmed, and the wheat industry being ruined, by the very same tariff protection that is enabling manufacturing industries to be temporarily prosperous.
I think it is opportune for us to mention that the prosperity which eastern industries' are enjoying is purely temporary. Once you ruin the west there is bound to be a reaction on eastern industries, and you will have them closing up; for one of their greatest markets is western Canada. If you do not give the producer of the west a fair price above his cost of production, it is bound to have an adverse effect on eastern industries. The letter goes on:
If the tariff protection enjoyed by manufacturing industries is to remain at the present high level, so as to ensure that all existing Canadian industries (many of which were brought into being and only exist to-day by reason of these high tariffs) are to be kept in being and prosperous, then it is a sad lookout for Canadian agriculture, and for our western wheat industry in particular; for it finally means that 2-j million people in the prairie provinces

far more than are employed in all the Canadian manufacturing industries put together-will be condemned to an extremely low standard of living, lower perhaps, we suggest, than peasantry itself.
There is another point to be considered, too. What about the continued prosperity of manufacturing industries themselves? If foreign markets for our western wheat are to continue to be curtailed-as they certainly are curtailed to-day by Canadian high tariffs-then the purchasing power of 2 i million people, a most substantial market for eastern manufactured goods, will automatically be curtailed in proportion. High tariffs, therefore, while they raise the cost of production of all farmers, and curtail drastically the sales of wheat, if continued will certainly inflict serious harm upon Canadian manufacturing industries themselves, and so upon all their thousands of workers.
When one adds to these evils, the high cost of arming for war-the direct result in turn of high tariffs which restrict international trade-one wonders whether high tariffs are of any permanent value to any one!
By this bill, which we are about to give its third reading-or rather, which the Liberals are about to see shall pass, because they have the majority to force it through-we are compelling the farmers to accept a price which is bound to cause bankruptcy and ruin throughout the west, which will put our people, who are a reasonable, aggressive and industrious people, back into the position of peasantry; and, as the Searle report indicates, there will be worse consequences even than that. The question is so serious that I think it should be reconsidered by every hon. member and the price raised to at least 80 cents.

-the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas) was discussing this matter from a purely political point of view. He was attempting to impress upon this house the contention that this bill is setting a price of 70 cents to the farmer. It has been stated over and over again since the debate opened that no attempt has been made under this bill to set a price for the farmer. I think what I read to the house last night from the statement of the then prime minister, in placing the legislation of 1935 before the house, will convince hon. members that at that time there was no intention of setting a price to the farmer for his wheat. The intention, then, as now, was to set an initial payment or initial price. The whole intent was an initial payment, which we have always known in western Canada as an advance.
To bear that out I might remind the house that a definite set price in the bill was asked for at that time. I think I am in the memory of hon, members when I say that the definite

Canadian Wheat Board
price asked for was 95 cents. Even when the advisory committee met with the board, which was appointed I think in July, 1935, in order to discuss this matter the question between members of the advisory committee and the board itself was as between an 80 cent advance and a 95 cent set price. I need only recall the fact that the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan), speaking during the campaign of 1935, stated to his constituents in Montreal that a much higher price than 87^ cents had been asked for, and that the government was responsible for making it 87i cents rather than the price which had been asked, which as I said was 95 cents.
As a matter of fact one particular group was advocating a set initial payment of 80 cents. Another group was advocating a set price of 95 cents; and the government of the day established an initial payment of 87| cents. They justified that figure on the ground that it bore some relationship to the world price of that time. In the remarks I read to the house last night the reason for that is clearly indicated. The prime minister of the day indicated that it was intended by the legislation of 1935 that all the- facilities which had been set up for the handling of Canadian wheat, both in Canada and in Great Britain, were to be given an opportunity to continue to operate. This bears out the contention that an attempt was made at that time to set an initial payment, not what would eventually work out to be a final payment for the wheat of western Canada. That initial payment was kept somewhere in relation to the world price for the further purpose of making it possible for farmers to market their 1935 crop without that marketing being interfered with by what might be paid for the carry-over from the crop of previous years.
I say this in order to indicate that an attempt was made under the legislation of 1935, and is being made under this legislation, to establish an initial payment, not to establish a price that the farmer is to get for his wheat for this or for succeeding years.
I tried on one or two previous occasions to emphasize that the only reason for the wheat pool not being able to operate in previous years was that it followed the price upward on a rising market but was unable to follow it down on a falling market. Those who are accusing this government of sabotaging, or attempting to sabotage, the wheat board- and the hon. member for Weyburn used that term a little earlier in the debate; those who spoke the other night of the government
attempting to betray the farmers of western Canada-that term again was used by the hon. member for Weyburn; those who referred to the present activities of the government in relation to this question as a shabby deal for the farmers of western Canada, are in the company of those who at the present time are attempting to sabotage the wheat board by exactly the same methods as the wheat pool was previously sabotaged.
There are only two ways by which the wheat board can ever be prevented from operating continuously in western Canada. One is by setting the initial payment so high that all the taxpayers of Canada will have to pay a considerable part of the price paid for the wheat every year. If any section of this house or any section of the grain trade of western Canada-not the grain trade but the operators of facilities in western Canada, who by the way financed the whole campaign of opposition to this program, financed the sending in of the resolutions that were sent in, financed the newspaper campaign in connection with it-I say that if there is any group of individuals who are engaged in sabotaging the wheat board it is the men who are attempting to force the initial payment so high that the remainder of the people of Canada will not stand for that payment. That is one method by which it can be done, and the surest.
What is the other method? There is only one other method by which the wheat board can be sabotaged, that is by the farmers themselves refusing to deliver their wheat to the board. My hon. friends talk a great deal about the desire of the farmers of western Canada for a wheat board. They talk sometimes of the desire of our farmers for wheat pools. Others talk of the desire of our farmers for certain other bodies through which to market their grain. But the farmer himself by his action shows what he desires to do in connection with the marketing of his wheat. If the farmers of western Canada desire to maintain a wheat board in operation all they require to do is to deliver their wheat through the facilities to the wheat board at a reasonable advance and a wheat board will be kept in existence. If a reasonable advance payment be provided for under that board and they be allowed participation in any profits made over and above the advance payment as the wheat is sold during the remainder of the year, that is what the man who really believes in a wheat board is asking for. And all those who believe in a wheat board in those terms-and they are the only people who believe in a wheat board-have an opportunity of doing that thing under the

Canadian Wheat Board

bill which we are now considering. If they do not desire to operate under that bill, they have the further opportunity of operating under bill 82, which makes provision for the setting up of central selling agencies over which they themselves have absolute control and under which also they have an absolute guarantee from this government of an initial payment of 60 cents. Those who believe in the pooling of grain in western Canada consider this to be a sufficient guarantee to induce every farmer who actually believes in that method to put his grain under an organization of that kind.
In addition they have under the legislation which is yet to come before this house, in the form in which it has come back from the committee, a measure which will control the' grain trade as it has been in existence through the grain exchange for a number of years. For the first time in the history of Canada every wheat grower in western Canada has the option of choosing among the three different methods of marketing grain which have been advocated in western Canada by different sections of the farming population. At least fifty per cent of the farmers of western Canada show by their actions that they still believe they can market their grain to the best advantage through the open market system. They proved that when the pool was in operation; they proved it in 1935 when the board was in operation, and they will prove it any year when the initial payment is established at a level which bears a reasonable relationship to the world price for wheat. The other fifty per cent of the farmers in western Canada have been divided in their opinion. Perhaps the majority of them believe a government wheat board can market the crop of those who believe in cooperative marketing to better advantage than any other organization. Perhaps a majority of them believe that they can set up and control an organization of their own to handle the marketing of their grain to better advantage than in any other manner. But whatever they believe, under the legislation brought into this house this session the farmers will have the opportunity of determining for themselves what form of organization they desire; and the only people who are trying to sabotage that one choice, that of continuously marketing their grain through a wheat board under the control of the federal government, are those who are continuously advocating a price so high that no federal government will be able to maintain it over a term of years.
I want to tell the hon. member for Wey-bum, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) and hon. members from

Alberta and anywhere else that none of us on this side who represent constituencies in the wheat growing area have any qualms of conscience about going out to the prairies and placing the program that has gone through this house this session before the farmers of the west, and resting our case with them. Never before in the history of grain growing in western Canada have the farmers been given the opportunity of deciding for themselves-apart from the agitation carried on by a bunch of paid agitators, to whom we in the west have become accustomed-exactly how they want to market their grain. If they want to market it through a wheat board they can establish that fact by delivering their grain to the board under a 70 cent guaranteed advance. If they do not desire to do that they can indicate their wishes by the fact that they do not so deliver their grain; and if in that way they indicate that they do not want their grain handled any longer by a government board then they have the opportunity of proceeding under bill 82 and setting up their own voluntary organization to handle their wheat. If they do not desire to adopt either of these methods they may still choose to sell their grain in the open market. This session the house has placed these three choices before the farmers of western Canada, and we are prepared to abide by the decision of those farmers as to the system they prefer. No one on this side of the house has attempted, by any word or action, to sabotage the wheat board or do anything that may be detrimental to the farmers of the west. We have attempted to help them in solving their problem of marketing their grain, and we believe this legislation will help. I would suggest that this bill be given third reading, that we stop playing politics with. it and send it over to the senate where it may be dealt with.

What steps is the minister taking to investigate combines that affect the high cost of living in Canada, combines in commodities, many of which have been referred to in the house? There may be a coal famine this winter, and I should like to know what steps the government proposes to take under this or some other statute, perhaps holding an investigation under the Inquiries Act, to reduce the high cost of living in Canada and the high prices charged for many articles in ordinary domestic use. Surely if ever there was a time in the history of this country when the government should do something to reduce the cost of living, it is now. Surely the minister who is in charge of the Combines Investigation Act can find some other way of doing things than by reference to the province or the municipality. As it is now, there is a reference to almost everybody, and I know of no regulatory body that is doing anything to bring down the high cost of living or to deal with the high rates of interest, which is a subject we have discussed on many bills that have been before the house this session. Surely parliament, having spent millions on commissions since 1900, can do something practical for the working people of this country engaged in industry in the cities or in agriculture.

I can only speak with respect to the investigation of combines. municipalities in respect of the work they are doing in cooperation with the work of the mounted police in the cities and towns at this time under the present emergency which confronts the empire? Take the city of Toronto; it is costing us a lot of money to maintain the police force. In New Zealand and in New South Wales the governments make grants to the cities by way of subvention or subsidy to help them to maintain law and order. With the increasing use of the pistol, life is not safe to-day on the by-ways of any city. Surely the government should cooperate with the municipalities to give the civic taxpayers some relief, in view of the number of people who are being attacked and injured, victimized by burglars, struck by motor cars, and so forth.
In connection with sabotage and mischief of that kind the mounted police are doing excellent work in Toronto, but there should be definite cooperation. As a matter of public policy, there is, but too much of the cost of police work is placed upon the municipalities. Then along comes the province and the same thing happens. The police system is costing the taxpayers more. than they can stand. If the government has at heart the interests of law and order, as I know the minister has, recognizing that the criminal code is being extended all the time to new offences and new conditions, surely the government can give a grant to the large municipalities to help them maintain their police forces and cooperate with the mounted police in the enforcement of federal statutes; otherwise enforcement will be very ineffective. speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think
the plea of my hon. friend might be more properly addressed to the provincial government. The municipal police forces are under the provincial governments^ I mean that the municipalities are the creatures of the provinces, and there must certainly be coordination and cooperation between provincial and municipal forces. If we tried to invade that field we should certainly be charged with trespassing upon a jurisdiction which is not ours. In many, indeed in most provinces, the provincial authorities have made arrangements with the federal government to the end that their policing shall be done by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, and it works very well. But I do not think it will be possible for us to

Supply-Justice-Mounted Police
do anything along the line suggested by my hon. friend in Toronto or elsewhere in Ontario. It is for the provincial and city police to apply the laws and regulations.

Ordinarily I agree with the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) in many of his submissions with reference to Toronto, but I suggest to the minister that to give effect to his philosophy in this matter would be to impose on the law-abiding communities of Canada who make their contribution to the federal budget and revenue the special burden of taking care of offenders in cities whose educational and moral progress is retrograde in that it produces within their boundaries wrongdoers who ought to be controlled by local police. In considering the appropriations for the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, we must have regard to the fact that they are the force upon whom we rely for our secret service activities in Canada. They are the force upon whom we rely in the main for the larger national protection of public services and industries if war were to threaten or to break out, and upon whose shoulders lies the responsibility for combating sabotage. During the last war their activities were tremendously effective, protecting as they did the Welland canal against foreign attempts to destroy it, protecting the Revel-stoke tunnel on the Canadian Pacific railway, protecting against sabotage activities key and basic power plants and industries the maintenance of which is so important. To permit these forces to be broken down to assist cities, such as the one represented by the hon. member for Broadview, in the control of their local bad men, would be entirely to take away the national purpose and effort of this great force of which we are all so proud.

I suggest that the mounted police should be especially well drilled and trained with regard to that part of the code having to do with the carrying of offensive weapons. When we come to deal with the criminal code, I hope the minister will see fit to amend it in such a way that a good many less of our citizens will be permitted to carry these offensive weapons. The reply from Mr. Mann was that he had not provided that information. The federal representative at Edmonton said he had not furnished it either. I should like the minister to tell us where he got the information.

It is on the file the
hon. gentleman has, which is the return brought down this session, showing that I got it from the Alberta government.

Would the minister tell
the committee the system followed in the distribution of this relief in Saskatchewan? While I am on my feet I want to ask the minister another question. It will be recalled that on one occasion last year I asked if the minister would table the report of Doctor Stapleton on his investigation into the whole system of relief and the distribution of relief in Saskatchewan over a period of years, up to, I think, 1936. I am asking this question in view of what took place in the province last year, and particularly in the northern part. Is it possible to have the report?
I think it is possible to table it. I will inquire before the general estimates are brought down.

Item agreed to.
Governor general's warrants.
1,90. To provide for a contribution to the international commission for the assistance of child refugees in Spain (governor general's warrant, November 4, 1938), $10,000.
Will some one tell the committee whether any Spanish child refugees came to Canada, or if there are any here now?

No. This grant was not for the purpose of bringing Spanish children refugees to Canada but was a contribution to a general fund gathered through the instrumentality of an international commission sponsored by the League of Nations. A request was made of the government to contribute something to the general fund by way of food supplies. We contributed $10,000 and delivered fish around the early part of the year.
Did we contribute only fish? Did we send any wheat?
No, only fish.
Is the total amount used up?
Yes.

It is too bad, because there are all kinds of Canadian child refugees in the city of Hull who are in need of relief. Will the minister consider using any portion that has not been used, for Canadian refugee children in the city of Hull?
May I interrupt the hon. member? There is nobody suffering in Hull.
I would like to contradict the hon. member, because I have had them up in my room this afternoon. They are people cut off relief.
The hon. member does not know what he is talking about.

I will bring them here. Item agreed to.
Governor general's warrants.
491. To provide for compensation to owners of animals slaughtered under the Animal Contagious Diseases Act (governor general's war-want, November 23, 1938), $120,000.

I should like to congratulate the Minister of Agriculture and the government upon the cooperation they gave us when we put on tuberculin tests in our district. Whole herds of cattle were wiped out because of tubercular infection. We have received splendid cooperation, and had it not been for the vote I do not know what those farmers would have done. I have seen splendid herds
3964	COMMONS
Supply-Governor General's Warrants
of cows, of twenty-six or more, condemned by the government inspector. Those cattle were costing the farmers more than they were worth, but when they were condemned the farmers received compensation which enabled them to buy cattle to take the place of those which had been destroyed.
Has this not been voted for the past ten or fifteen years? Have we not for some time compensated farmers for cattle which had to be slaughtered?

Yes, farmers have
received compensation in this respect for a number of years.
Does this vote provide for expenditures in any new districts, or does it apply only to the districts affected last year?
The vote provides for expenditures in the last fiscal year. Any amounts for new districts this year will be in the further estimates.

Item agreed to.
Governor general's warrants.
To provide, under agreement with the province of Ontario, pursuant to the provisions of the Unemployment and Agricultural Assistance Act, 1938, for a program of special works for the purpose of assisting in the alleviation
an emergency unemployment condition in the northern sections of the province (governor general's warrant, December 14, 1938), $1,000,000.
Would the Minister of Transport or the Minister of Labour give the details as to what this amount was used for, and where it was used?

This warrant was issued to meet an emergency situation in northern Ontario, which arose because of a very serious curtailment of employment in the woods in that section of the province. I believe it is estimated that the cut this last winter has been about twenty-five per cent of the normal. Therefore about the beginning of December of last year we had to meet a condition brought about because thousands of men who normally found work in the woods were congregating in the cities and towns of that part of the province. We felt the situation could best be met by carrying on certain highway work in northern Ontario in the winter months.
Would the minister give me the details?

Note: Although the total of the above maximum dominion contributions exceeds $1,000,000 it is understood that this approval does not increase the maximum dominion contribution of $1,000,000 authorized by the agreement.

Has the minister at hand the total amount spent in northern Ontario in the last year by the dominion government? Then, if he has the figures of amounts spent by the province, I should like to have them.

I can say only that the total of 81,000,000 provided under the warrant was expended for winter work in the period from December 1 to March 31. Previous work in that area last year did not come under the Department of Labour. When the estimates of my colleague the Minister of Mines and Resources are before the committee I am quite sure he will be able to supply that information.

I am informed that at the present time much of the work in that northern section, around the constituencies of the Minister of Transport and the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River, has been closed down,
and the contractors are simply waiting for something to turn up. I met one of the contractors in Montreal the other day, although I believe he is a resident of Toronto, not of Montreal. He said, incidentally, that he had been doing work in, I think, the constituency of the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River, or in any event in some part of northern Ontario, as I learn from Fort William that a good deal of the work up there has been shut down, and that the contractors are not busy. This man from Toronto told me that he was merely waiting, and that if nothing turned up he was going to close his plant. He is keeping only a skeleton staff on the work.
As the minister said, last winter there was a scarcity of work in that section of the country because of the lessening of work in the bush. That was brought about because in

Supply-Governor General's Warrants
the previous year the pulp and paper companies cut too much and left themselves with an overload of pulpwood; so that last winter they cut very little and almost eliminated cam-p work. I am told a great deal of work is badly needed up there to keep the employees of contractors busy and thereby relieve the unemployment situation. The gentleman I mentioned described it to me in this way, that because this government is refusing to meet a like amount put up by the Ontario government, the provincial government is refusing to go on with the work. I am giving the statement, of course, as he gave it to me; I cannot vouch for its accuracy. I do know that there has been a good deal of complaint from the provincial government as to this government failing to give them what they consider is owing to them by the federal authorities. We had some differences ourselves in that regard, but we did put up a huge amount of money. I believe the item in dispute is quite large. I merely wished to say a few words on behalf of Fort William, and the Minister of Transport and the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River can speak for their sections. I do suggest that the Trans-Canada highway and mining roads in that section be treated as generously as possible. It is a large area of country; the territory from North Bay to the Manitoba boundary is as large as Germany and France put together, yet the population is small, and the conditions of distress are largely due to the overcut of pulp and paper. I urge upon the government that they give every consideration to further cooperation with the provincial government with a view to keeping these contracts going, so far as they can within reason, in order to help out conditions in that section of the country.

Being in close touch with the situation in northern Ontario, I might perhaps say a few words. There is great need for work this year in the area referred to by my hon. friend, and it is true that the highway work has not yet started, but if my hon. friend is familiar with the conditions he will realize that there is still a great deal of snow upon the roads in northwestern Ontario; in fact some of our airports in that section are still unusable on account of the snow. I think my hon. friend forgets the kind of weather we have there.
No, it is very much the same as here.

I was talking yesterday with a contractor interested in the northern highway program, and he told me that on account
[Mr. Manion.l
of the weather it would not be possible to resume work on a large scale until June 1.
The appropriations of the dominion for tourist, highways and mining are considerably larger than last year. As my hon. friend is aware, joint projects are carried out by the provincial government. It has long been the custom to ask the provincial governments to make allocation of the various projects, and we have not as yet received the allocation. We have advised the provincial government that we shall be very glad to consider allocations with them when they care to submit their list. There has been no friction between us in this matter.
My hon. friend referred to a claim of the provincial government which the dominion government has not paid. Shortly, the provincial government claims that the late government failed to pay about $14,000,000 on account of work done jointly during the regime of the previous government. We have not been able to find any agreement or justification for such a payment.
I admitted that there' was a dispute with the late government.

Yes, it was a matter entirely with the late government. As minister from that section of Ontario I feel very keenly for the citizens who are in distress, and the government is making every effort to relieve the situation there as rapidly as possible. Perhaps it was on my recommendation to the government that the situation last winter was relieved to the extent indicated by this vote. I am glad to say that recently the Canadian Pacific Railway Company has arranged with the Department of Transport to carry on a large program of rock ballasting work in that district. That work is now being put under ivay and is absorbing a fair amount of labour. When weather permits a resumption of road work, we hope the situation will be back to normal.

Speaking in support of this item, I may say that a small portion of this amount, matched as it was with a like amount from the province, was spent in my district of Parry Sound on road-making during the winter months. It went far towards helping out the unemployment situation, and produced splendid results for the money spent.
I feel that the item could be criticized rather on the score that it is not large enough than that there is any excess expenditure. When the appropriate minister comes with his estimates-I think it will be the Minister of Mines and Resources rather than the Minister of Laboui-he can very properly put in a substantial allowance, to be matched again

Supply-Governor General's Warrants
by Ontario, for continuation of road work in the northern parts. Dollar for dollar value is being received for the money expended, and the expenditure goes a long way toward reducing the relief rolls.
Lest it might be thought, from what the hon. gentleman has said, that I was criticizing the item, let me say that I am not opposing it at all.
No; I understood the hon. gentleman to have commended the item.
That is right.
Is the Minister of Labour aware of the appalling condition of destitution and poverty that exists in Hull, and would he consider using any of this money to relieve the terrible distress over there?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member is out of order.
If I may interject, Mr. Chairman, at the proper time I can give my hon. friend information that he needs regarding the city of Hull.

The remarks of the leader of the opposition have elicited most of the information I desired to have. May I, however, ask the Minister of Labour who determines the allocation of this money? Unlike the hon. member for Parry Sound, I can say that none was spent in my district, and that is one reason why I want some information with reference to its allocation, and to call the attention of the minister to the fact that within 150 miles of Ottawa conditions are just as emergent as they are in any part of northern Ontario.
As to the contention that the work is necessary and that it encourages tourist traffic, this government started on a policy three or four years ago of helping to build feeder roads from the Canada-United States boundary line into northern Ontario. There lie between the Ottawa river and the St. Lawrence many roads which were started under that policy and were given provincial and federal aid, but they have not been completed. With reference to the policy of road building, while this grant of $1,000,000 perhaps met an emergent condition last year, there should be continuity of policy in this regard. In my judgment it is poor business to build patches of road here and there and have no continuity of policy over the years which would ensure their completion. As it is now, it is a matter of patchwork, building a piece of road here and a piece of road there. The federal treasury is making huge grants, and it should have some say
where the money is to be spent. If we had some definite policy with reference to road building and our assistance to the provincial government in that regard, and at least a fifty per cent say as to where the roads should be built, we would be a good deal further ahead in the long run. If a grant for road building comparable to this is made this year, I hope the Minister of Labour will stiffen his back a little and that some work will be done in areas where roads were started a few years ago so that they may be brought to completion.

The amount voted by the dominion government was applied to projects which in the opinion of the province could be carried on usefully during the winter months in the areas where distress existed. In other words we left it to the province, subject to our approval of course, to indicate the projects which could be carried on usefully and at the same time relieve this unemployment situation. As for the larger question raised by my hon. friend, there will be an opportunity, I am sure, to discuss that when the estimates of the Minister of Mines and Resources are before the house later.

I am certainly in favour of this vote. Last winter, when it was decided to spend a certain amount of money in northern Ontario, I was to some extent disappointed at the way the money was divided. I supposed it would be divided almost equally, considering that the situation is of almost equal gravity in all the ridings of northern Ontario; but I found out that there was a difference. I must, however, give credit to the Minister of Labour for having rearranged the distribution of that money.
I do not think the hon. member gave him enough credit. He gave him only a million dollars.

We do not expect too much from a political Santa Claus. We gathered enough experience to enable the government to remedy next fall any errors which may have been made. If moneys are to be given from the federal treasury next year and work is provided in the cutting of a right of way over the trans-Canada highway, or for roads in some sections of the northern country, we shall know what can and cannot be done before the snow is out of the way. Before that time it was found almost impossible to cut a right of way properly; one can visualize how hard it is for an axe man to cut stumps and clear the ground when we have four or five feet of snow as we had last winter. We shall gain from that experience. I hope it will be found possible first to build a camp, and second to open a lot
<3968	COMMONS
Supply-Governor General's Warrants
of gravel pits on which it will be possible to give some work to our agricultural population. We are not aifected so grievously in mining sections such as Sudbury. I am not speaking with any particular knowledge of that section, but I have reference more to the Porcupine section. We certainly need help in the Hearst and Cochrane sections, and a great deal can be done in employing settlers and their horses in useful work which will provide them with decent roads when the snow is gone.
I wish also to compliment the government- I do not know from what direction the orders were given-in that we always held that we were the missing link of the trans-Canada highway. I echo the fine words which the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) uttered a few moments ago with regard to the work done in his own section of the trans-Canada highway. I believe it is due to the Minister of Labour that this winter there was started a real program of work on the trans-Canada highway, particularly west and south of the town of Hearst. We are going to be able to go north at Cochrane and Kapuskasing, also from Hearst and then to Oba, where you come in touch with the north shore of lake Superior.
Again I would compliment the department or whoever is responsible upon the inauguration of that work. It has not been the solution of all our problems of unemployment, but it is a step in the right direction. The work will be enlarged in following years, and we shall have gained from the experience of last fall and last winter.
How many men have been given employment on that particular project? What was the rate of wages paid, and how many days a week did each individual work?

I will answer the hon.
member in so far as I have the information here.
The men-days worked were as follows:
Men-days
January, 1939	 41,609
February, 1939	 96,245
March, 1939	 123,323
Total	 261,177
That is the equivalent of the employment of 3,600 men for a continuous work period of three months. The wages paid were the prevailing wages in the district in which the work was done in accordance with the practice followed in highway work.

What are the prevailing
wages in that district which were paid on that work?

I have not the information at hand now, but I will make a note of it and provide it to my hon. friend if we have a record of it here. I am not sure that we have, because actually the work was done by contractors under the provincial department of highways.

The wages paid were
the prevailing rates for provincial government men employed in that section of the country.
But does not this government insist on a certain rate on any projects in respect of which the government is giving financial assistance?
They were all satisfied.

It is stipulated in the agreement that fair wages shall be paid, and they are regarded as the prevailing wage in the district where the work is done. I can assure my hon. friend that the inspectors see to it that this stipulation is strictly carried out.

The hon. member for
Parry Sound does not know whether the men were satisfied or not. I am sure that he would not be satisfied if for his work he was paid what those men got.

I interrupted to say that
there was no dissatisfaction-
How do you know?

-with the prevailing
rate, because I took some trouble to know about the expenditure, and about the men who were taken off relief and went to work on this job. I challenge my hon. friend to name a single man who is dissatisfied with the two million dollars spent.

The item before us is
for one million dollars.

The hon. member has
been told already that the province matched it with another million. Two million dollars were spent.

Quite so. There was no
suggestion in my mind, and I do not think the Minister of Labour misunderstood me, that there was any exception taken to the rates paid. I was asking, merely for my own information, whether on this work, as should be the case in all work of this kind, the wages paid were equitable and sufficient to keep those employed.

Well, the hon. member
has the information.
Item agreed to.

speakeroldname: Hon. IAN MACKENZIE (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: INTERIM SUPPLY
speechtext:
When we were last in
committee we were discussing item 208, but there was an understanding amongst all members that there should be a general debate without restriction when the item was called again.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. J. MANION (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: INTERIM SUPPLY
speechtext:
As the minister says, it was
the understanding that we should discuss in general the whole question of defence under this item, and in the long run I think it will save time to do so; because if one were forced to divide one's remarks into various parts the debate would likely take much longer. I have no desire at this late stage to delay the committee, but this question of defence in general, which has caused very much discussion throughout the country, is in present world conditions of the greatest importance. There will be, as there should be, a considerable debate upon it in view of the magnitude of the main item-$63,000,-000-and its importance to the dominion.
I listened the other day with a great deal of interest to the minister for about two and a half hours as he gave details of the work of his department, and it is with some dif-
Supply-National Defence

fidence that anyone like myself attempts to discuss a subject of this kind; it is a matter that calls for far greater expert knowledge than I pretend to possess. But I do wish to indicate in a general way the feeling which I believe exists throughout the country with reference to this matter particularly.
From my reading and conversations I have had with those who claim to be experts, I believe it is the general opinion in Canada among military men who are well posted that we are not properly prepared in any way to defend ourselves should there be a world war, that we are unfortunately not in a position to protect ourselves to any great extent. The minister, it is true, gave a great many items indicative of the preparations that have been already carried out, but he also submitted a long list of requirements that are on order and some that are still to be requisitioned, which would seem largely to support the idea that our defence is not in very good shape. May I admit at once that it is due to the laxity, if I may use that word for want of a better, of all governments for a long time back; though I do believe that the present government came into power at a time when world conditions were changing. Because world conditions were changing, and possibly because of the fact that our government did little in this matter; the present government deserves to share more of the responsibility than either the government that preceded them or the government of my hon. friends which preceded us before 1930.
We have spent in the last three years something like $90,000,000; we have in the estimates this year something over S60.000.000, yet it seems to me we are only now getting prepared for possible repercussions if a world conflagration takes place. Now on the eve of an election, this government, having been in power for four years, are taking precautions which I believe should have been taken earlier. It seems that in almost everything the government do they lack a distinct plan or method. The wheat bills that we have just been dealing with are a good illustration; they have been changed four times at any rate within the last few weeks, if not the last few days. The unemployment and youth problems have not been adequately dealt with,
I noticed an item in the press this morning regarding the putting up and taking down of flags and decorations in front of this and other government buildings. Even in the matter of putting up a few flags the government seem to muddle it.

subtopic: INTERIM SUPPLY
speechtext: Order.

subtopic: INTERIM SUPPLY
speechtext: What is the point of order?

subtopic: INTERIM SUPPLY
speechtext: The item under discussion has nothing to do with the subject with which my hon. friend is dealing.

subtopic: INTERIM SUPPLY
speechtext:
I know as much about order as my hon. friend, so that I shall probably go on without being called to order by him.
In regard to defence, we have just the same type of indecision as in practically everything else with which this government have dealt. It is true that they give in reply the old tu quoque argument. They say that between 1930 and 1935 we did nothing. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) shakes his head, but the other day the Minister of National Defence devoted a considerable part of his two and a half hour speech to showing that between 1930 and 1935 we neglected to put up the defences that we now complain this government has not put up. I admit it at once, but I could if I wished go back to the period 1921 to 1930 and show that in those nine years the Liberal government which preceded our Conservative government neglected it in the same way. I consider that the Liberal government between 1921 and 1930, and our government between 1930 and 1935, were excusable on this ground, that the whole idea of disarmament was general throughout the world from 1920 until about the middle nineteen thirties. There was a desire not only for physical disarmament but for mental disarmament. The Minister of Justice, who makes a study of international affairs, will recall the Kellogg-Briand pact of August, 1928, which put on record the desire or determination on the part of the great countries of the world in future to settle all international disputes by peaceful means rather than by warfare. It was the spirit bf the times. That same spirit continued until the early nineteen thirties, right up to about the time we went out of office. In fact it was not until at least 1935 that there was really any marked change. I was at the disarmament conference of 1933 and I met there representatives of many countries. All of them were determined if possible to bring about a disarmament treaty; they were very hopeful of its being brought about-England, France, all the countries they represented. That was the spirit of the middle nineteen thirties, and that feeling lasted until at least 1935. Hitler's rise had then begun-I think he became chancellor in 1933-but the world generally did not realize the possibilities of international discord that his coming would bring, did not realize the danger that would arise from that type of dictatorship. It was

Supply-National Defence
late 1935 or early 1936 when the Rhine was refortified and Germany began to rearm. It was then that Great Britain and France really awakened to the danger. Great Britain began to build up an industry of the utmost importance to the British Isles, and it was then that I think we lagged; we should have copied Great Britain-perhaps not immediately, because after all Great Britain is right on the edge of the volcano and we are farther away. But long before this time we should have realized that there was need for more defence provision than we have at the present time.
On top of that we have made a mistake even this year, when we have begun to show signs of life; we have begun badly with the Bren gun embroglio and the Janin contract, which I do not intend to discuss now. In building up the industries of our country and utilizing them for the making of munitions the start was made in a bad way. For example, to-day, as the minister told us in his speech, we have something like four anti-aircraft guns-I think that is what the minister said.

subtopic: INTERIM SUPPLY
speechtext:
There
were four ordered by my predecessor; at the present time we have fourteen altogether in Canada.

subtopic: INTERIM SUPPLY
speechtext: Well, I may have misunderstood what I read in the minister's speech.

subtopic: INTERIM SUPPLY
speechtext: The figures vary from time to time.

subtopic: INTERIM SUPPLY
speechtext:
But I understood the
minister to say, dealing with anti-aircraft guns, that we had only four.

subtopic: INTERIM SUPPLY
speechtext: May I give my hon. friend to-day's figures? Fourteen on hand and 18 on order.

subtopic: INTERIM SUPPLY
speechtext: Let me read the minister's words and see wherein I was mistaken.
