speechtext: My information at that time was probably about two months old.

subtopic: INTERIM SUPPLY
speechtext:
On page 3243 of Hansard the minister is reported as saying:
By March 31, 1939-
Only a month and a half ago.
-the following orders had been completed: four 3-inch anti-aircraft guns ordered in 1935 have been delivered.
Then on page 3245 he said:
As to anti-aircraft equipment, answering the question of my hon. friend a few moments ago, they were ordered by the previous administration and since then there have been ordered 14 anti-aircraft guns of the 4-5-inch calibre and 4 of 3-inch calibre for future delivery, at an estimated total cost of $1,289,240.
The member for Royal (Mr. Brooks) then asked:
When does the minister expect delivery?
And the minister replied:
I think fairly soon, but I cannot be specific in regard to that.
Have they been delivered since?

subtopic: INTERIM SUPPLY
speechtext: No; these are naval anti-aircraft guns. In addition to those ordered by the hon. member for Yale when he was minister, there are 14 now awaiting delivery in Canada-18 plus 14.

subtopic: INTERIM SUPPLY
speechtext: My impression, from information obtained from men who are well posted from a military standpoint, who have studied the question, is that we would need to use in round figures probably 100 antiaircraft guns.

subtopic: INTERIM SUPPLY
speechtext: I think 124.

subtopic: INTERIM SUPPLY
speechtext:
Well, then, we need at least 100 more than we have. I doubt whether to-day, in the present state of international affairs, there is any equipment we require more than anti-aircraft guns, because if war broke out and we were attacked by a foreign country it would be an attack by air; it would have to be that. While a ship might come across the ocean and bomb some of our ports, it could do nothing of importance further than that without the use of aircraft. So that if there is any article of warfare that is badly required at present in this country, it is what I have mentioned-anti-aircraft guns. The minister says we would need about 124, which sounds reasonable to me, because we would require them on both coasts and some in the centre of Canada for fear of possible attack from Hudson bay and James bay.
In addition the minister said we have thirty-six modern service aircraft and about 174 others that are either obsolete or are training aircraft; in other words they are old-fashioned boats that can be used for training purposes only. I imagine it would be suicide to send any men up in them to compete with modern aircraft coming, say, from an aircraft carrier that entered the St. Lawrence or James bay or other adjacent waters. So we have thirty-six effective planes, and if you spread those out in the sections of Canada where they might be needed you would have perhaps twelve on each coast and twelve around the centre of Canada, which I imagine would be about one-fifth or one-tenth of what we should have.
So, Mr. Chairman, I suggest that this government should have profited by past mistakes; by our mistakes, those of the last government, if you like, and by their own

Supply-National Defence
mistakes when they were in power from 1921 to 1929. I submit that it should not have taken the government four years to realize that we had made a mistake in thinking the world was going to be peaceful when in fact the world has no semblance of peace at the present time except in so far as there is not actually a war taking place, with the exception of the one in China.
I am merely touching these points in a general way, but I come next to our navy, which is weak in the same way. That is probably the fault of all of us; we were all against spending large sums of money on a Canadian navy. Again, however, for the last four years this has been the responsibility of the present government. The minister says we have six destroyers with 4-6 inch guns, and it has been stated by authorities that one cruiser with 6 inch guns could drive these destroyers off the sea. Yet we are one of the great trading nations of the world. Our import and export trade in round figures I suppose is worth a total of a thousand million dollars a year; yet we have practically no defence against anything like a heavy enemy ship coming across here, after perhaps breaking through the British navy and the United States navy, if the United States were in the war, and attacking the focal points where our trade converges, say at Halifax, Saint John and up the St. Lawrence, and on the other coast towards Victoria and Vancouver.
There are a few suggestions I should like to make, again in a general way. In the first place I agree with the minister's statement that we need fear no danger from the south.
I do not think the English-speaking nations are in any danger of ever fighting among themselves, either Canada and the United States or the United States and any other part of the British empire. I feel that if such a war ever took place it would be akin to fratricide, and I do not think there is even a possibility of anything like that happening. So our defences must be on the east, the west and the north. We have a long coast line, all of which is vulnerable to a certain extent. It is true that our geography does not change, but unfortunately military science has advanced very greatly, so much so that distance has been largely annihilated. We have reached the stage in warfare when machinery is much more important than men; indeed to-day an army without machinery would be slaughtered in very short order if it had to compete with an army well equipped with the machinery of war.
That we are in danger from the air seems very evident, if only from the fact that the 
United States itself has been spending huge sums on protection from attacks by air, in the construction of aircraft, anti-aircraft guns, and so on. Generally speaking no enemy airplane would find it reasonably feasible to attack the United States without passing over some portion of Canada. Therefore the fact that the United States is vulnerable to air attack or at least they think they are so \ulnerable that they are building defences- shows that we are much more vulnerable due to the formation of our country and the shorter route around the northern section of the globe. Our terminals, our ports and our trade routes are all vulnerable to foreign attack. I pointed out in other discussions in this ^ house, I think during the Bren gun discussion for example, the danger from James bay. I do not want to repeat what I said then, but an area from Quebec on the east to Winnipeg on the west would be within range of airplanes brought into James bay by an enemy ship. In that area we have the industrial and political hearts of the country. Therefore we must go on doing all we can, as rapidly as we can, to increase our defences. It would seem to me that our anti-aircraft supplies are most urgent. I am not sure of the order in which I am putting these matters, but I would say the aircraft themselves would come next. The minister has his orders in, and I hope we all realize the need of pushing these orders forward to completion as rapidly as possible.
In addition to protecting our ports and our trade routes we must be in a position to protect our neutrality should the oft-quoted possibility of a war between Japan and the United States ever materialize. We have an indented coast line, with many islands, which would be ideal for use by an enemy country as a base for submarine attacks; and if we could not protect our neutrality, with a country like the United States fighting for its very life, we would be in a difficult position if we allowed our coasts to be used by enemy ships.
Then we must build up a nucleus for all the different branches of the service. That is being attempted, and I Should like to see it go forward much more rapidly.
Another very important matter that has been neglected is the building up of our industrial life in a proper manner. As I pointed out a short time ago, about the middle thirties Great Britain realized the necessity of building up her industrial life in order to be able to supply her own needs in various types of munitions. In the same way, on a smaller scale, we should be doing the same thing. We cannot buy these things, at any

Supply-National Defence
rate to any great extent, from any other country in the world to-day. We might buy some material from the United States, though it would be too bad to have to do so if we could make them ourselves, as we can. We cannot buy them in England at present, because England may have to fight for her very life, and she requires all her industrial power to manufacture supplies of one kind and another for herself. In this country we have the ability, the ingenuity, the engineering skill and the financial power to build up a great industry of this kind. From 1914 to 1918 we did magnificent work along these lines. I was looking up a speech I made some time ago in connection with another matter-I do not remember the subject of the debate-and I am going to quote a statement I put on record at that time, coming from the British war cabinet and put out after the last war, showing the possibilities of this country for building up a great industry and supplying ourselves with munitions. At page 1870 of Hansard for this year I quoted the statement of the British war cabinet at some length. This is what they said:
Dealing at this juncture with production, as it had been in 1917, the British war cabinet declared that "the manufacturing resources of Canada have been mobilized for war production almost as completely as those of the British isles," and added these detailed facts. . . .
Fifteen per cent of the total expenditure of the ministry of munitions in the last six months of the year was incurred in that country.
That is, in Canada. Then the article goes on:
She has manufactured nearly every type of shell from the 18-pounder to the 9-2-inch. In the case of the 18-pounder, no less than 55 per cent of the output of shrapnel shells in the last six months came from Canada, and most of these w-ere complete rounds of ammunition, which went direct to France. Canada also contributed 42 per cent of the total 4-2 shells-
Then they go on with more details which I shall not put on the record. In the next column this statement of the British war cabinet gives complete figures with regard to quantities, of our exports during the four years. I said:
There are a good many other details w-hieh I do not wish to put on record, but I think these are worth while:
"Shells	 65,343,674
Fuses	 29,638,126
Fuse parts	 16,174,073
Cartridge cases	 48,627,673
Percussion primers	 35,386,488
Shell forgings	 6,412,115
Explosives; chemicals (lbs.)..	111,297,107
Metals; compounds (lbs.). ..	107,282,336
Lumber (feet)	 53,327,107
Exploder containers	 13,285,000"
Then I say the statement goes on to deal with the matter complimentarily in greater detail, during the four years of the war. Speaking roughly, that was the stupendous amount of production which Canada put into the war zone. It was a magnificent piece of work. In the review from which I quoted on the other occasion it would appear that they could give no praise too high for the splendid' work which was done during those four years in mobilizing our industrial activity for the purpose of building up a great industry to supply the allies with ammunition of various kinds.
At the present time the world is unhappily in such a condition that we have once again to consider the same line of business. It isa very unhappy circumstance that we should have to do so. I do not suppose there is anybody in the house who believes more in peace or is a more sincere anti-war person than I am. At the same time I am not one who believes that we can remain defenceless when the rest of the world is building up defences. A condition which, although it has no bearing on the matter, may be considered as being akin to it, would be that suggested by some of my hon. friends to the left. They suggest that we should remain free trade when the whole world is protecting itself against our exports. I believe the two situations are similar. We must follow the line taken by the rest of the world.
Consequently I submit it is a great opportunity for Canada and a great opportunity for business to build up. It is a great opportunity to relieve our unemployment situation. I say the government is to be criticized for not having grasped that fact much sooner than it did. It is true the minister told us, in another speech, that some 1,500 industrial plants have been surveyed for the purpose of mobilizing our industrial strength. But so far as I know the mobilization of industry has not been proceeded with to any great extent. We have even antagonized industry by the very contracts to which I referred a few moments ago, namely the Bren and Janin contracts, where no competition was brought into the picture from big manufacturing corporations, of which I know, which would be open to consider such contracts. Therefore I say we have so far missed an opportunity, of which advantage can still be taken, and which I emphasize strongly should be taken advantage of at the earliest moment.
In addition to building our own supplies, there are undoubtedly great opportunities for us to use our great industrial works to supply other countries, particularly Great Britain.
Supply-National Defence

We realize that Great Britain is sitting on the edge of the volcano, and is in a position where she requires to build up her defence with the utmost speed. If we have the industrial development to meet the requirements of Great Britain, then we have an opportunity to help her not only as part of the empire but to meet her needs of supply. I am informed that New Zealand and Australia have got much farther than we ha-ve along the road of supplying themselves with munitions. Surely with our great industrial plants we can go more deeply into this matter, and do it with the utmost speed. We require aeroplanes, munitions, artillery, mechanical transports, tanks, armoured cars, tractors, rifles and machine guns, to name only a few of our absolute needs.
Someone has said that the industry of a nation governs its military strength. To build up an industry or at least to convert it from its ordinary work into the work of manufacturing munitions and war supplies takes time. Consequently I feel that the government have been far too slow in this work, and that we should move forward with the utmost speed to catch up, as England is to-day catching up, on the neglect in the early days of the nineteen-thirties. People did not then realize, as we did not, that the dictatorships would soon be endangering the democracies of the world. And so, if needs be, we must be ready to mobilize our industrial strength in war-time.
Then, in a speech I delivered some weeks ago I suggested that we should have something by way of a committee of the house and the senate for the purpose of consulting with the present defence committee which exists in the Department of National Defence, to go into matters which cannot be dealt with quite so fully in the whole house or in a committee of the house as they could be in a small committee of that kind. In such a committee there could be the utmost secrecy, and details could be given. I believe that is a matter which is well worthy of consideration by the government. That committee could be made up of some of the members of the House of Commons and of the Senate who take a particular interest in this matter.

All the more reason, then, why we should have it. We would be able to go into detail that we cannot possibly place before the House of Commons, for reasons of national interest, if you like.
I admit it is unfortunate at a time like this when we could utilize our wealth for the constructive development of the country and to develop it along lines of peace, that we should even have to consider defence expenditures such as we have before us. But we have to take the world as we find it. We are not in control of the international gangsters who are to-day endangering the peace of the world. And because of the fact that they do endanger the peace of the world we have not only to protect our ideals but to be ready to participate, if we must, in self-defence, in defence of our ideals, of the empire, and of world democracies in general.
Once more when the world is again calm, as we hope it may be in the near future- although at the present time there is not much prospect of that condition-Canada may again lead the way towards peace and disarmament. Of course the trouble has been that science has gone ahead so rapidly that the 3,000 miles of ocean which we always looked upon as a barrier is no longer an effective defence. Consequently we must have these different types of armaments for our defence.
I should like now to say a few words about our militia, in general. After all, it is the oldest arm of our defence, and I think it is still a dependable one. There is no doubt that in the last war the militia was the great arm of defence. The development of war in the air was an important factor, but the militia was so important that if either side had been deficient in it the war would have concluded much sooner.
There are the two branches, namely the permanent and the non-permanent forces. I have nothing to say about the permanent force. In the permanent militia in the Department of National Defence we have in Canada a splendid group of men. From the days of the hon. member for Rimouski (Sir Eugene Fiset) we have had a splendid group of men giving their lives to the keeping together of a skeleton force of men, to which they may add when occasion arises.
But I do not believe any of us have given sufficient attention to the non-permanent

Supply-National Defence
militia. There is no doubt that it has been neglected. I remember that when I sat on the government benches we were criticized because of expenditures, no matter how small they may have been, for the non-permanent force. True, to-day there cannot be the same criticism there was at that time, because I believe even the greatest pacifist in Canada must realize the changed condition in the world. But we have all neglected that branch of the service. There has been a group of loyal and energetic officers who have shown devotion and self-sacrifice for the non-permanent militia, and who have given, of their time and money to help the organization along. But they have not been able to get from any of the governments, either the one to which I belonged or the present one, sufficient clothing, boots or supplies for the men. I was glad to hear the minister mention in his speech that there is more being done in the wray of handing out supplies of boots and clothing. It was shocking to learn-and I confess I did not know it until the minister stated it-that in the past few years the non-permanent militia had been dependent upon supplies left from the last war, which ended a little more than twenty years ago. It seems extraordinary that there should be any part of them left. These splendid men who have built up the non-permanent militia at their own expense and by their own selfsacrifice and energy should be assisted to build it up in a stronger way. I care not what pacifist suggests that we should not have military training; I sincerely believe there is no finer training for a young man than something in the way of military training and discipline. Far be it from me to suggest anything in the way of being warlike, but I believe that young men in military training get a discipline and physical fitness that they cannot get anywhere else; and when young men are willing to join the non-permanent militia and take part in parades, it may be, and drills and training, we should give them every encouragement, and encouragement also to the officers who have done so much by their own efforts to help build up the organization. The estimates for this branch of the service are about the same as last year.

The minister in his speech said that there was a turn-over of about 50 per cent in the non-permanent militia. But 50 per cent seems pretty high, and I believe it is because the men felt dissatisfied with the clothing and boots with which they were being supplied. I want to assure the minister and through him the government that in any encouragement he gives to either the permanent or the non-permanent militia I shall be very glad to support him because that is the foundation upon which we must build in time of need.
This is not the time for a debate on international affairs, and I do not intend to indulge in such a debate. But world conditions are such that it is necessary for us to protect our nation and our national ideals. It is also a time when we can build up an industry such as I have suggested, which will be for the defence of the country and give employment. I am told by a friend of mine who was in Hamilton recently that he was advised that in that city some of the steel plant employees and employees in electrical plants were being laid off to add to our out-of-works. That is the very type of employee who would be of the utmost use to us in this new industry which it is possible for us to build up.
What strikes me is that if unhappily an international conflagration should break out, we are not only in danger but largely defenceless. I do not think that is an exaggeration. There has been very little done to correct the state of our defences, and never was there a time when we had a better opportunity to correct it than now when there is so much unemployment, with half a million unemployed men in Canada. That offers a splendid opportunity for the government to stop fiddling and get down to business seriously. We have the ability, we have the need. Therefore we have the opportunity, and the government should awaken and push this matter vigorously, show more courage than it has done, and more than we showed, for that matter, between 1930 and 1935. But

Supply-National Defence

at that time, I repeat, there was not the call for it that there is now. After four years in office this government should get down to doing what is urgently required and do everything it can to supply to-day's urgent needs.
There is one other matter to which I wish to refer in a sentence. The minister mentioned cooperation with the British government in regard to the training of pilots, and said that some fifty British pilots would be trained over here. In the British isles they speak of pilots in such huge numbers that fifty seems to be merely a fleabite. I think that opportunity might well be broadened to give pilot training to a very much larger number if the British government desire it-not fifty, but hundreds and perhaps thousands. We have a huge area suitable for training of that kind. I am told that the reason why the British wanted to have us cooperate with them was that in their densely populated country there were dangers from aeroplanes crashing and all that sort of thing, whereas we have wide open spaces capable of furnishing miles and miles of training area which could be utilized without danger to the civilian population.
I suggest that we cooperate with the British government to the utmost possible degree in that regard. If there was in the past any reason for not doing so, it seems to me that reason has gone. The Prime Minister, the Minister of Justice and I, from different sections of the house, took the same attitude with regard to cooperation. I do not think the Prime Minister was as clear-cut as he might have been ; but after listening to him and then to the Minister of Justice in regard to the absolute impossibility of Canada remaining neutral in a war in which Great Britain was engaged-an attitude which I took just as they did, or at least as the Minister of Justice did; for I might say, after hearing the two speeches of the Prime Minister and the speech of the Minister of Justice, that was their attitude-I believe the attitude of the government is that we must cooperate with Great Britain to the fullest possible extent short of conscripting our men to send them overseas. I take the same attitude myself, and since we have taken that attitude, it seems to me that the government might well forget the position they took in the past, if it is that which is holding them back, and cooperate to the fullest possible extent with Great Britain in the training of British pilots over here. Certainly they will receive no criticism from me or from this party if they cooperate with the British government in that matter,

and I think much more should be done than is indicated by training only fifty pilots.

Then I make no further comment on that. Before resuming my seat I wish to say that I support the department and the government in any constructive defence plans for this country. The democracies must stand collectively together, as I stated in the house on another occasion. If ever there was a time in the history of the world when democracies should stand shoulder to shoulder, it is now. We must try to secure ourselves, in a sense, collectively. I frankly admit to-day that I have not much faith in the power of the League of Nations, but it is the only organization we have that acts as a sort of forum at which the different nations meet. Therefore I should not like to suggest our getting out of it, but rather, through it or by some other method, we should endeavour, all the democracies of the world, to work collectively together to protect the ideals of free speech, free parliamentary institutions, individual freedoms and freedoms of other kinds which we possess and which the dictator countries do not possess. Whatever our faults may be-and we have many in the handling of our affairs; many of them have been pointed out by various people in the last year or so-despite them all I would rather be as we are than be regimented as are the people of Germany, Italy and Russia, and I think our people generally, if they had the choice to make, would take exactly the same attitude. The only protection we have against international gangsterism is that we should stand together as democracies shoulder to shoulder. If we do not do that, there is a danger, and, to my mind, a great danger, of the dictator countries conquering in the end. I do not even like to think of such a possibility.
In closing, let me repeat that I am ready, and this party is ready, to cooperate with the government in constructive methods for building up a munitions industry in this country, for building up our defence forces, and utilizing this $63,000,000 in the best interests of Canada as a whole.

Mr. Chairman, when the estimates of the Department of External Affairs were taken up, there was a protracted debate, in the course of which every phase of our foreign policy was discussed. The latter is linked up with national defence and with the expenditures that are necessary for its maintenance and development. The Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion), the right hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), as well as group leaders, former ministers and many hon, members availed themselves of that opportunity to define their stand and to lay down before the people of this country the results of their investigations.
During the last few months, great events have engaged our attention; a disturbing, ever-recurring thought, which is almost an obsession, is preying upon our minds and compels us to ask ourselves: Will war break out? Shall we succeed in preserving peace? The world is in a state of turmoil. Night and day, at every hour and every minute, the radio and the press give us news despatches, and acquaint us with governmental discussions, rumours and comments; on all sides there is in evidence a state of unrest reminiscent of the conditions that prevailed before the catastrophe of 1914. Having scarcely recovered from the trials we underwent at that time, we are now being threatened with a still more severe ordeal. That state of mind is reflected in our debates, as is shown by the twenty-six speeches delivered during the debate on external affairs. In listening to them, we were reminded of the fact that parliament is truly a place where people speak-and at great length. In that respect, our system of government, availing itself of all its rights and privileges, is faithful to its traditions. In the years to come, should any parliamentary historian or chronicler with leisure and a good deal of courage, wish to deal with those discussions, a reference to Hansard will enable him to realize the labours of the people's representatives. He will note, I am sure, that no problem escapes their attention, and that they know how to analyse and solve it.
When we look over the policies of the British government, and the relationship between the latter and the dominions, our minds are exercised mostly over the momentous decisions that would have to be taken in the event of a European conflict in which Great Britain might be involved. In dealing with those various matters our thoughts and actions must be governed by certain leading principles.
We must choose between three courses: neutrality; participation with or without con-71492- 250i
scription; and non participation. The legal aspect of the first course has been thoroughly discussed. The question has been put whether or not Canada is empowered to declare her neutrality, and whether her parliament may decide to wage war or to preserve peace. Opinions vary to a great extent. As always, our legal lights are pointing in opposite directions. While the endeavour to define a right is commendable, it is more important to face the facts and to act accordingly.
However, two distinct theories have been evolved. The supporters of the first one state that European wars are no concern of ours since they arise from the clash of economic, financial or political interests; that the Berlin-Rome axis corresponds to the England-Erance axis, soon to be joined by Russia, each one of those groups endeavouring to court the favour of small nations; that all through the centuries, wars have resulted from the old seesaw game of treaties and alliances; that the negotiations leading to those treaties and alliances are not submitted to us for consideration and approval; that we are acquainted with decisions taken, outside our knowledge and without our consent, and without our having a say in the matter. According to that school of thought, we are not bound by such decisions and our neutrality having been declared, we must resort to the most complete isolation. That is the policy which is invariably followed; the decisions are taken by the British government and they are afterwards communicated to us.
In this connection, we must remember the speech delivered by the prime minister, Mr. Chamberlain, in the British House of Commons, on the 13th April last, after the occupation of Albania by Italian forces. After reviewing certain events which had occurred before that serious incident, he said:
Consequently, they have come to the conclusion that, in the event of any action being taken which clearly threatens the independence of Greece and Roumania, and which the Greek or Roumanian governments respectively consider it vital to resist with their national forces, His Majesty's government will feel themselves bound to lend at once to the Greek or Roumanian governments, as the case might be, all the support in their power.
We are communicating this declaration to the governments directly concerned and to the powers, especially Turkey, whose close relationships with the Greek government are known, and I understand that the French government are making a similar declaration this afternoon.
I need not add that the dominion governments, as always, are being continuously informed of developments.
The second theory is that of intervention or participation in European wars as soon as England and her ally, France, have decided upon war, either for the preservation of the
Supply-National Defence

independence of Greece, Roumania or Poland, or-those two countries wishing to remain world arbitrators-for helping them to fulfil that ambition; that should they be unable to achieve it by themselves, at their own expense and risk, we must go to their aid, not only in organizing our own defence, but in putting expeditionary forces at their disposal; that such forces must be kept in readiness through every means, even through conscription; that we must exhaust our resources in man power and money in order to maintain democratic ideals on the European continent and ensure the freedom and independence of those countries that are threatened by fascist and nazist doctrines; that such sacrifices will be necessary if we are to continue enjoying our freedom on the American continent.
There are some who bring to the study of these problems a great deal of logic and common sense, whereas others cannot seem to rid themselves, in this regard, of the influence of passion and prejudice, with the result that there ensue acrid discussions and controversies which threaten to cancel all our efforts toward national unity. But the decision will rest, in the final analysis, with parliament.
To the domestic policy, on which we were not agreed, is now added an external policy which multiplies our disputes and fans the flame of dissension.
We are being called upon, this year, to vote a considerable increase in the National Defence estimates. In making our decision, we must keep in mind the sole interests of this country, not forgetting to take into account the events of the last few months which have endowed the situation with ever-increasing gravity. Whether we wish it or not, these events are bound to affect us and we cannot afford to ignore them. They impose upon us new obligations, the first of which is to increase and develop our armaments in view of our country's defence. This idea is opposed in certain quarters where it is feared that such armaments would inevitably draw us into new adventures. "What is the reason, they add, for this huge expenditure, and against whom are we arming''?
Every citizen has the duty of defending his country. Now he cannot accomplish this duty unless he is furnished with the adequate means of doing so. The advocates of neutrality which, they feel, parliament should proclaim, cannot assuredly allege that this neutrality should not be protected in case of aggression. It would be most unwise to wait until this happened before looking about us for some means of protection. It would then be too late. One usually protects one's self against accident and illness hazards by taking out an 
insurance policy, which does not necessarily mean that the insured shall fall ill or be the victim of an accident but that, should he be stricken with illness or fall victim to an accident, he shall be properly safeguarded against the consequences thereof. It would undoubtedly be far better not to be forced to insure ourselves against such hazards, yet it is equally wise to pay the premiums and make sure that we are protected. The same rule applies as regards the defence of our country. It is not after an attack has been launched, nor war declared, that we should resort to arming ourselves. In truth, all these precautions shall not prevent further assaults against our peace of mind, unless the hope expressed on March 31 last by Major Vernon Bartlett, independent member of the British parliament, should come true:
We shall not be able to enjoy ourselves until Franco's widow tells Stalin on his deathbed that Hitler has been assassinated at Mussolini's funeral.
I am aware that, in the province of Quebec, a campaign is being waged against what is termed the armaments race, and that it is being said that this increase in the estimates has no other purpose than the sending, in case of war, of an expeditionary force to Europe.
According to the advice of experts, any such attempt, in view of modern armaments and especially the development of aerial and submarine warfare, would end in disaster. Neither Canada, nor the United States could, as was done during the great war, land troops in France or in England. This opinion is shared by all those who, without being experts, are aware of the grave peril to sea navigation which bombers and submarines constitute. It is perhaps not irrelevant to mention here the despatches we have all read to the effect that certain members of the British cabinet were of the opinion that the King should cancel his trip to Canada. They feared that, should he cross the Atlantic under present conditions and war be declared while he were in Canada, he could not return to England before the cessation of hostilities. The following cable dated London, April 15 last, was recently published in the Montreal Standard:
The Sunday Express said to-night that some members of the cabinet are attempting to persuade King George to cancel his scheduled visit to Canada and the United States this summer.
There is a sharp division of opinion whether Their Majesties should make the tour at all or not. Certain ministers feel that if there even is a possibility of a war within the next two months the king and queen should not be allowed to cross the Atlantic.

Supply-National Defence
Were a war to break out while they are on the American continent there might be no possibility of their returning to Britain until the hostilities ceased.
Not only are those who oppose the defence appropriations obsessed by the idea that an expeditionary force is to be sent overseas, but they persist in stating that armaments will lead to our participation in external wars and, therefore, to conscription. In order to alarm public opinion, they keep recalling what took place from 1914 to 1918 and say that we are heading for similar catastrophes.
They insinuate that those who are in favour of providing for the defence of the country want war and that those who oppose any increase in the defence appropriations are against war. This unsound reasoning can only create disunion by means of which certain undesirable elements seek to obtain control.
In 1937 I obtained from my electors of Lotbiniere the mandate to sit in this house. I did not seek it under false representations; it was given to me with full knowledge of the facts. National defence was the main issue. I maintained everywhere that it was our duty to organize the defence of the country and to vote the appropriations required for that purpose. I pointed out that this expenditure was not made with any idea of aggression, but solely to repulse any attack from the outside and to protect our neutrality.
When in 1938 I had the honour of moving the address in reply to the speech from the throne, I made identical statements. I added, however, that if we were to impose heavy sacrifices upon ourselves in order to maintain and develop our means of defence, we did not intend to participate in external war nor, above all, to spend a single dollar for the dispatch of an expeditionary force beyond the ocean. I was of the opinion then, as I am now, that measures of national defence, within our means, are a sufficient participation; that when all the parts are properly defended the whole is sufficiently protected. Such a defence cannot be improvised; each year new circumstances compel further efforts.
War is a horrible thing. Must we, to avoid it, abstain from all defence preparations? Must we remain in splendid isolation, counting on our neighbour to come to our assistance in the event of our being attacked? It is well for us to rely on our neighbour, but, in order to obtain his help in war time we have to show beforehand our intention to do our part.
From time immemorial the world has wanted peace, but invariably, at fixed periods, wars have broken out. More than ever treaties are but scraps of paper thrown into the wastepaper basket according as interest or ambition dictates. It is unnecessary to cite instances remembered by all.
During the past year the statements and actions of Hitler and Mussolini have been such as to make us not only anxious but prudent.
It is well to remember these words of a great statesman:
Peace is nothing but the more or less prolonged interval required to get ready for another war.
More than a century ago, in 1807, Talleyrand wrote:
When all the talk is of peace, that is the time when it is necessary to prepare for war more than ever and to multiply resources.
Governments live by the sweat of their brow. That is a universal law. In these troublous times heads of governments have great difficulty in getting their sincerity recognized. Their clearest statements are questioned; they are charged with the blackest intentions; suspicion and doubt is raised about them.
Why should there be any doubt about the explicit statements made by the Prime Minister at the imperial conference in London, in May and June, 1937? Why doubt his more recent statements made on March 30 last, concerning conscription:
One political fact is equally clear: in a war to save the liberty of others, and thus our own, we should not sacrifice our own liberty or our own unity. Planning and coordination would be essential, but the necessary coordination could be made, and if this government were in power it would be made, without sacrificing those vital ends and conditions of our existence. Profits could and would be rigidly controlled, and profiteering suppressed. But men's lives and men's wills cannot be put on the same basis as goods and profits. The present government believes that conscription of men for overseas service would not be a necessary or an effective step. Let me say that so long as this government may be in power, no such measure will be enacted.
Why should it be thought that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) was not sincere when the following day, speaking on the same questions, he said:
Reason, judgment and the interests of the country must predominate.
The French Canadians will never agree that any government has the right to force them to military service on the other side of the ocean.
I think I am true to my concept of Canadian unity when I say that I shall always fight against this policy; I would not be a member of a government that would enact it; and not only that, but I say with all my responsibility to the people of Canada that I would oppose any government that would enforce it. I agree with what was said yesterday by the leader of the opposition and the Prime Minister, and what was said by Mr. Bruce of Australia, that
Supply-National Defence

the time for expeditionary forces overseas is certainly past, and it would not be the most effective way to help our allies. The men would be needed here; and in any event it is parliament which will decide about it.
We should take reasonable measures, within our means, to protect ourselves from possible attack, at least while we are waiting for outside help; we must have some means of helping ourselves.
Can any statement of principles be more formal or any engagement more absolute?
Should the government's actions prove to be at variance with the above statements, the people will appreciate and judge. Their verdict cannot be doubted.
I have always considered that within the ranks of a party it was not necessary to worship the leaders, but only to trust them. That requires a certain discipline. This discipline, indispensable to any common action, while keeping us in the limits of intelligent leadership in no way diminishes the sincerity and strength of our convictions; it does not prevent criticism of leaders-in fact, leaders should invite criticism and seek to profit by it, so long as it relates to matters of policy. The exercise of this freedom of thought, of speech and of criticism is the basis of true liberalism. However, we should avoid the kind of criticism that degenerates into wrangling, for then, outward appearances of wisdom ill conceal intrigue and weakness which make one the victim of compromising associates and of dangerous and unscrupulous backers, whose sole purpose is to ensure the success of their electoral propaganda.
More than ever if we wish to maintain our parliamentary system is it necessary to submit to leadership. Some years ago, probably foreseeing the dangers which threaten the democracies to-day, a French statesman, Raymond Poincare, speaking of the need of a sound political system, said:
The difficulty is not to set out on paper a long list of legislative resolutions. Usually, such lists are simple enumerations of future failures of election promises. There is one thing which is at the same time harder to attain and more necessary, that is, to apply to the daily study of the successive problems arising from the normal run of political life that community of mind and of ideas upon which, to a far greater extent than upon the deceptive identity of formulas, rest the strength and cohesion of parties. That unanimity of resolve, that spontaneous agreement on guiding principles are not attained without the sacrifice of some personal opinions to the common will. The governing principles upon which unity is achieved should never be forgotten. The leaders must initiate all important decisions and accept their responsibility with courage; their authority should not be based on expedients and opportunism; they must manfully adopt a policy looking to the future; their aims must be lofty and far-seeing. All must understand that failing organization, method and continuity lMr. Francceur.]
of purpose, a party, no matter how generous its intentions might be, is doomed to tergiversations, disorder and helplessness.
Our leaders have "initiated all important decisions and accepted their responsibility." The easier course would have been to cajole the people and adopt methods which are being brought into use for the purpose of getting votes at the next election. It is an easy way of getting applause.
I might be permitted to quote the words of a writer who has defined the character of a leader in the following words:
Those who look for cheap applause are not real masters-neither of themselves nor of those they want to lead. Mob enthusiasm is easily raised by cajolery, by a flow of words, by high sounding and empty formulas whose flourish dazes and intoxicates, because the mind is saved the hard work of thinking. In that manner mobs are easily swayed but they are not carried very far. At the first onslaught, the ranks give way, are shattered and thrown In every direction. The character of a leader bears a different stamp. It is a moving spirit because it is a motive power.
During the debate on the address, the hon. member for Argenteuil (Mr. Heon) delivered a speech which excited some interest in the province of Quebec. He concluded his speech by the following declaration:
. Let us be frank and face the facts. Participation <in a continental war will, whether we want it or not, be an issue at the next general election.. It will most certainly be an issue in Quebec. I could not escape it in my own constituency even if I tried.
He made no mention of other most important problems which surely will be the subject of long discussions during the electoral campaign.
His leader, however, if he is to be judged by his propaganda, does not appear to make an issue of that problem in the province of Quebec. On the 19th of April last, for instance, the hon. leader of the opposition sent to the electors of my constituency, apparently over his own signature, a circular letter covering the speeches of the hon. Messrs. C. Senn, W. Earl Rowe, T. A. Thompson, and J. H. Harris, on the importation of vegetable oils, and on the live stock and dairy industries.

Thompson, member for Lanark; Mr. J. H. Harris, member for Danforth. Mr. Harris reviewed the question in great detail on March 18 and 24, 1937.

The Conservative party has always taken the interests of the Canadian farmer and to-day as ever continues fighting so that he might be treated fairly.

This evening this committee has passed seventeen bills of divorce; this is the eighteenth. I have strongly protested against this practice, which is shameful. I cannot understand how the respectable members of the Senate and the House of Commons can stand such dirty and stinking legislation. It is clear in nearly every case that the evidence has been fabricated either by the parties or by the investigators, who are experts in keyhole business. They can see, from a distance and through a keyhole, anything that is done. It is the same story of the sheets raised to their shoulders, the bottle of Scotch half empty, the two glasses, and the rags on the chair. Then they come with evidence which is no evidence, and the hon. gentlemen of the senate are satisfied with it. After reading the evidence which is agreed to favourably by the senate, I would not recommend any one of them to the Minister of Justice for appointment to the bench. It is clear and evident that the so-called evidence is just a fake, yet it is agreed to by the other house. Here we swallow it without tasting it, but it smells very bad and I object to it. We shall have the royal assent given to some bills next week, and I hope that his majesty will not be called upon to sanction any one of these dirty bills. In fact, I know personally that he will not, and I praise highly the government for not putting those bills before his majesty, because if they did he would get disgusted with this parliament.
Order.

My hon. friend says
" order"?
Yes, certainly, the hon. member should know better; he should not mention his majesty's name in connection with such bills.

I mention him because I respect him, and my hon. friend should know better than that himself. I find that this business which is being done at the present time by the Senate and the House of Commons is shameful. I said so before without any protest from any member of this house, because the hon. gentleman who now speaks was not present at the time. But now that he is in he should acquire better manners.

He should think of his father and his mother, of his grandfather and his grandmother, who did not behave in that way.

On a point of order,
I demand that the hon. member withdraw that statement.

If I withdraw the statement it will mean something insulting towards his ancestors, which I do not mean. I have respect for them, as the hon. member should. As the hon. member for Parry Sound (Mr. Slaght) said so aptly, there is a time to finish all this. Why do we have this divorce business? It is just to give some fees to the lobbyists who pay a licence fee of $25 to the clerk of this house to go round and make $500 on each case of divorce. That is all; and as they are friends of all governments, they keep that business for years. In order to give that soft and juicy pear to some pests, we are putting ourselves to shame. What member of the house can decently hand the statute books of this country to anyone who is not familiar with our system of legislation without knowing that Canada has been discredited in all countries of the world in this connection. It is time, sir, to stop this shameful practice. Look at the statute books of this country, the laws governing each man, woman and child in Canada. At the end of the book there is some private legislation. It is not so considerable now as it was for a time, but it is still too great; even one of these divorce bills would be too many. We have something more important to look after than bills of this kind. It is time we stopped this sort of thing, and the only way to stop it is for the senate to refuse to accept such legislation. It is up to the senate not to accept any of these bills when they come up for first reading and to tell the sponsors to go somewhere else if they want legislation of this kind.
I say that, Mr. Chairman, with deep conviction and because I have respect for this house and for the senate. I also have respect for the governor general, and I do not want him to put his name on such legislation. Therefore, sir, I hope the wish expressed by the hon. member for Parry Sound and others of my colleagues will be followed, so that in future we may be relieved of this rotten, dirty, stinking legislation.

We have had two members of the legal profession speak on this question, and I agree with them that we shall have to watch anything that tends to break down the home life of the country. I think this is an argument that the province of Quebec should
take care of its own home life and not send here that which, if we would call a spade a spade, is a type of legalized prostitution.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Transport):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to be considered as intervening in opposition to this bill. I do ask, however, that it be studied by a committee of the house that has had some experience in dealing with matters of this kind. Hon. gentlemen will recall that last year a similar bill was debated before this house for many weeks, and that so much opposition was shown to it that, while it passed this house, it was withdrawn in another place.
These bills are very important. After all, this proposed legislation authorizes an expenditure of some $4,500,000. It gives a franchise for a definite period of three years, but according to the wording of the bill as long as seven years may be taken for the construction of the bridge. The bridge may be located at any point within five miles either way of the harbour of Prescott, the other

Prescott and Ogdensburg Bridge
end being in or near the city of Ogdensburg. The project also gives a United States company the right to take over the whole project and award the contracts, although it is specifically provided that half the labour and half the materials shall be of Canadian origin. So I say I am not opposing the bill, but I do ask that it be studied carefully.
I appreciate the fact that in this house we are not supposed to refer to proceedings in the other house. But as the report in the other house was practically an instruction to this house I think I am entitled to read a few words from the debates of the senate for Wednesday, May 10.
Is that a report on this bill?

Yes, on this bill. It is a report of the committee on railways and shipping, by its chairman. Right Hon. George P. Graham. At the end of the report we find these words:
The committee had the gentleman in charge of the bill agree that a deposit clause should be inserted in the bill. As time was so short, it was agreed that this clause should be inserted in the commons, although this is a senate bill.
I read that because I think the second house to consider the bill might reasonably assume that the first house had gone fully into the substance of the bill and had attended to all matters of that kind. I cannot imagine the reason for the haste in the other chamber with respect to a bill having the importance of this one. It was literally put through over a weekend. I might say that I instructed my law officers to attend the committee and give me a report of the proceedings. The bill was put through so rapidly that my officers were unable to find the time and place fixed for the committee to sit, and so failed to attend.
I therefore ask the committee of this house to give this bill the consideration that a bill of its importance deserves. I quite concur in the motion for second reading, and would suggest that the bill be referred to the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, which has dealt with similar bills in the past.

I wish to add only a few words to those of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Howe). I ask that in the committee the bill be given consideration from two points of view. Hon. members will recall that recently a bridge known as the Thousand Islands bridge was constructed, in the county of Leeds, at a point probably thirty or forty miles distant from where it is proposed to construct the bridge designated in this bill.
Bridges are desirable in connection with tourist traffic, but I submit that this house ought not, without careful consideration,

authorize the construction of a second bridge which may have the effect of destroying the value of the investment of those who have invested money in the one recently built. These bridges cost a large amount of money, and from the point of view of justice to those who have already constructed a bridge we ought to consider carefully whether or not we would authorize the construction of another bridge which would practically destroy the usefulness of the first one. That, however, is a matter to be decided between the two companies.
I wish to point out that the bill authorizing the construction of the Thousand Islands bridge and the bill before us each contain a section providing that when the obligations of these companies are satisfied by tolls from the bridge, the bridge then becomes public property and free of tolls. In that connection I would point out that if too many bridges are constructed, the time when they will be free of tolls will be long delayed. All I ask is that the committee consider these matters, from the point of view of fairness to both the company which has already constructed a bridge, and the public, which desires to have these bridges free of tolls as soon as possible.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and referred to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines.
