The house in committee of supply, Mr. Sanderson in the chair.
General.
208. Adjustment of war claims, $60,000.

When the committee rose at six o'clock, I was comparing the international situation as it existed in May and in July, 1938 and as it was in January, 1939, when the national defence estimates were brought down in this house.
In the light of these facts and statements, can we not conclude that while events in Europe justified the greatest pessimism in the spring of 1938, the outlook was more favourable in January, 1939?
There was still, to be sure, the matter of colonies. But that claim was not new. Let us remember Hitler's provoking and defiant words in the spring of 1938, as compared with his courteous language both in November and in January last.
On November 8, Hitler, speaking in Munich in the presence of thousands of soldiers had this to say:
We have many times stated that we have no claim against France and England, except the return of colonies which were taken away from us without any regard to right. But I have always asserted that this could not, of course, lead to war. . . . With that exception, we have no claim against these countries and we do not ask them anything.
Then, on January 30, 1939, in the Reichstag, chancellor Hitler made it clear that between Germany, France and England there remained ony a colonial dispute to be settled, but that it was not worth while going to war on that ground.
Whatever the situation in Europe may have been in January, 1939, Canada was still an American country. In what respect then, was Canada in itself more threatened than at the end of May, 1938? In what way was she so much less protected that an increase of about 850,000,000 in the defence estimates should have been necessary?
Let us remember the opinion which the Prime Minister expressed in the speech which he delivered on May 24 last. After having stated that the situation in Europe was quite serious, he said:
It is unlikely . . . that at the moment, with the world as it is to-day any other country will single out Canada for attack. The talk
which one sometimes hears of aggressor countries planning to invade Canada and seize these tempting resources of ours is, to say the least, premature. It ignores our neighbours and our lack of neighbours; it ignores the strategic and transportation difficulties of transoceanic invasion; it ignores the vital fact that every aggressor has not only potential objects of its ambition many thousands of miles nearer which would be the object of any attack, but potential and actual rivals near at hand whom it could not disregard by launching fantastic expeditions across half the world. At present danger of attack upon Canada is minor in degree and secondhand in origin. . . .
I have pointed out that so far as we ourselves are concerned, being a country by ourselves, if we were confined to looking after ourselves we have little to fear.
The situation described by the Prime Minister in May, 1938 had not changed in January, 1939, and I wish this were better appreciated by those who are systematically attempting to stir up agitation towards war in playing upon the feelings of the people.
Such was, at any rate, in the opinion of the prime minister, the position of Canada as a country on May 24 last, and such it was too, on January 25, 1939, when the estimates were brought down-Canada was still less open to attack.
In fact, the three aggressor nations were no longer in the same position as the year before.
Japan needed all her strength to overcome the stout resistance which the Chinese have put up for almost two years; Italy still remained a negligible factor in so far as we were concerned; Germany, having established over Central Europe an economic domination which ensures her important markets, and the raw materials she needs, did not have to look westward, more especially in view of the fact that she would need aerial and naval bases which she does not have at the present time.
Of course, we could not' prevent a nation misled by ambitious leaders from launching into some mad and unpractical military venture, but, as the prime minister so forcibly explained on May 24 last " danger of attack upon Canada is minor in degree and secondhand in origin." Besides, chancellor Hitler himself pointed out to president Roosevelt on April 28 last, that, from a military standpoint, it would be sheer madness for him to dream of attacking or invading American territory.
Not only was Canada, as a country, less threatened, but she was better protected.
In the first place, our defence system had been improved. The thirty odd million dollars voted last year were used in strengthening further our defences.
In the second place, the president of the United States, Mr. Roosevelt, had given us the assurance that his country would extend her protection to us.
Supply-National Defence

Here is what he said in Kingston on August 18 last:
I give to you assurance that the people of the United States will not stand idly by if domination of Canadian soil is threatened.
He had on the same occasion recalled that, in a speech delivered a short time before in Brazil, he had included Canada within the "Fellowship of the Americas" with the warm approval of all nations of South America. In reasserting so emphatically that the United States were determined to protect Canada and to defend her against any foreign interference or threat-a gesture which he has renewed since that time-president Roosevelt warned those nations who might be tempted to attack us of the risk which such a venture would entail for them. Such a stand safeguards us against any serious attack.
In the third place, we had been given for our further protection, a declaration of American fellowship, known as the Lima declaration, which entailed the defence of American territory against any interference. In fact, in December last there was held at Lima, in the republic of Peru, a panamerican conference.
At the opening of the conference, the United States Secretary of State, Mr. Cordell Hull, made the following statement:
There can be no doubt as to the determination of the American nations to resist any invasion of this continent by the armed forces of any power or of any combination of powers.
And the final declaration at the close of the conference made absolutely clear the will of the American nations to resist any attack launched against any part of the American continent.
All these are formal guarantees of security which we did not possess a year ago.
Not only were we less threatened, and better protected, but we were in a more awkward financial position.
The budget deficit for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1938, totalled 117,715,368; for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1939, it has reached $55,000,000, and it is estimated that prospects for next year are even darker.
The Right Hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) made the following statement on February 27, during a debate at page 1359 of Hansard:
There are many works and reforms that I should like to have in my constituency, but the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) says that there is no money for them.
It is under such circumstances that the Minister of National Defence has moved and further moves that we authorize the expendi-
ture of $85,000,000 for armaments-that is, an increase of $50,000,000, notwithstanding the fact that during the last two years our defence system must have been considerably strengthened as the result of the large amounts authorized to that end.
What is the purpose of these preparations?
We are informed that the branch heads of the Department of National Defence (the militia, aviation and naval services) have requested that the government grant them much larger amounts than those set down in the present estimates, maintaining that those set down are far below present-day needs; that the cabinet had no way of ascertaining if these requests of the defence council members were as necessary as they claimed, and were obliged to accept without demur the statements of the various department heads with respect to their requirements. Information to this effect was given to us by the Prime Minister, in this very house, on March 14 last at page 1901.
Under such conditions, how can the members of this house decide, with full knowledge of the case, that our preparations are exclusively in view of Canada's defence? What is the real purpose prompting these department heads?
The Minister of National Defence stated to the house last year (cf. Hansard, unrevised edition, 1938, p. 1644) that there existed in this country five schools of thought, one of which, the imperialistic school, had as a slogan:
When Britain is at war Canada is at war and is bound to throw her whole weight into the conflict.
To which school of thought do they belong, those members of the defence council, those departmental heads, who want military appropriations "much higher" than $85,000,000, the necessity of which we cannot verify, as the Prime Minister has said? Do they belong to the imperialistic school, of which the Minister of National Defence was speaking, a school that would have us sacrifice our last man and our last dollar for the Empire, a school that places our first line of defence in Europe, in Africa or in Asia? Indeed, we are justified in thinking that those officials, in preparing the defence program, were not taking solely into consideration the defence of Canada in Canada, but, under the pretence of attending to Canadian interests, prepared our participation in external wrars.
As a matter of fact, all those in favour of our participation in extra-territorial wars welcomed with joy and enthusiasm the present military appropriation and asked for more, as did the departmental heads.

Supply-National Defence
The statement made by Mr. Chamberlain last February serves to confirm this belief:
Come the three corners of the world in arms, he said, and we will terrify them . . . with the aid of our army, our ships, our dominions and our loyal allies.
Nevertheless, we are still told that our preparations are for the defence of Canada, without, however, being informed as to where lies our first line of defence. The name and the thing itself are sometimes very different.
Nobody is opposed to the defence of Canada and to preparations for that purpose, but I am opposed to the defence of interests of others, at a distance of three or four thousand miles from our borders, and to preparations for such a purpose.
Was it a question of the defence of Canada when in September last the Prime Minister considered the possibility of summoning parliament with a view to taking effective and concerted action "in the event of war" breaking out in Europe because of a conflict arising in some distant country between peoples of which we knew nothing and to prevent a minority from obtaining its autonomy, according to the words of Mr. Chamberlain?
What then would have been the use of part of the preparations made during the past two years, supposedly for the defence of Canada?
Have we not double reason for suspicion this year, when our military estimates jump from thirty-four to eighty-five millions, while the old formula "When England is at war Canada is at war" is being revived? England is at present guaranteeing the boundaries of an increasing number of states, thus binding Canada to participation in their defence without the Canadian parliament having anything to say in the matter.
England, by reason of her interests and her engagements, has a thousand chances against one for Canada of being involved in war. It is therefore quite possible that our Bren machine-guns will be used for the first time on the battle-fields of Europe. After all, the possibilities of war, if any, exist in Europe or Africa, and not in America.
Last year, I rejoiced at the reduction of the estimates, compared with those of 193738; this year, we definitely enter in the armament race, which will lead us to ruin.
Mr. Chamberlain said, at the beginning of this year.
If armament expenditures continue, financial and economic ruin will follow.
Our military expenditures, already too heavy, are to be increased. Annual expenses arising out of the last war, and of our preparations, absorb nearly half of our total appropriations.
Let us give a thought to the generation of young men from twenty to thirty years who pay the price of the last war and cannot find work. I dare say that we are more secure against armed aggression than against a social crisis. Let us attend to the most urgent need. Otherwise, there will be disorder.

The statement of the minister on Canada's defence policy made it clear that there are two danger areas in Canada from the defence point of view-the Pacific coast and the Atlantic coast. Personally I think there might have been added to these two areas the St. Lawrence country in Quebec province.
And the Hudson bay.

And, as my leader says, the Hudson bay. It is also clear that each arm of Canada's defence force is being organized with these two danger areas in mind. For example, the navy is based on our two coasts. The air force, we learn, is divided into three commands: the western command, the eastern command and the central command- the latter, if I understood the minister correctly, being the reserve command. The two fighting commands of our air force are on our two coasts. We also learned from his statement that the military forces of Canada are allotted with the same plan in mind. For example, the minister stated, at page 3263 of Hansard.'.
The coast defence units are localized in the fortress areas concerned. The reserve units are localized throughout Canada, and have been allotted in accordance with population ratios.
The defence of these coast areas is vital to Canada, not only because there are Canadians there who would be subject to attack, but also because our great export trade goes from the shores of these two areas.
This evening I intend to speak from the point of view of the Canadians on the Pacific coast, one of the groups of Canadians admittedly most subject to attack; a group of Canadians who actually see fortifications being erected, guns being installed and air stations being built and who are directly interested in, and, I may add, gravely concerned over, the problem of the defence of Canada.
The minister stated that there are two types of attack Canada might face: first of all, major attacks; and second, minor raiding attacks. As against a major attack, he stated, we must depend on the Atlantic coast upon the British navy, and on the Pacific coast upon the United States navy and the great British base at Singapore, which, as we all know, was built and is being maintained by
Supply-National Defence

Great Britain, Australia, New Zealand, the Malay States and possibly other British territories on that side of the Pacific. But he went further and said that we must also depend upon these two fleets for the protection of our trade on the respective oceans: the British fleet on the Atlantic ocean, and the United States fleet on the Pacific ocean; and we have a great trade on the Pacific ocean going down largely from our coast to the Panama canal.
In the light of these definite statements, this government's announced policy on external affairs of "no commitments" looks remarkably like a policy of sponging. I suggest to the government that the time has come when we should hear no more about Canada having no commitments. Let us forget that policy, which was never a policy but only a bit of political camouflage. Actually the government are cooperating in defence matters to a certain extent with Great Britain and with the other dominions and the United States, but they seem afraid to admit that fact. I suggest that they adopt definitely a policy of open-I repeat that word, "open"-cooperation with these nations, two of which, according to our own Minister of National Defence, namely, Great Britain and the United States, are expected to protect us from major attacks; and I suggest that the government announce to the Canadian people this policy of open cooperation. There is too much hush-hush business about our policy on this question, and the Canadian people have been put in an unfortunate position. I illustrate that by quoting from an editorial in the Seattle Post-Intelligencer of April 14 of this year, part of which reads:
The undefended position of Canada has been a menace, not only to Canada, but to the United States.
This nation could not brook an attack upon Canada by an overseas aggressor. But it is manifestly unfair to expect Uncle Sam to guarantee emergency police service for neighbours able to bear a fair share of the cost of continental safety.
Canadians are a proud people, quite willing to do their fair share in proportion to their numbers and their wealth; and a definite policy of cooperation such as I suggest will enable them to retain not only their peace of mind, but also their self-respect, which is of vital importance to any nation. So much for major attacks against Canada.
The minister has said that there is another type of attack we might face-the minor raiding attack-and he has stated that against such attacks we cannot expect help but must depend upon ourselves. In other words we are thrown entirely upon our own resources.

Speaking again from the point of view of Canadians on the Pacific coast, I should like to make several suggestions to the minister and the government for the improvement of our Canadian defences. Let us take, first, our navy. Obviously, it should be strengthened; it is too weak for its job. On the Pacific coast we have four destroyers and two mine-sweepers. The minister the other night outlined the tasks of the navy; at page 3237 of Hansard he dealt with the need of patrolling our coasts and this is what we find, that the minister has been told by his staff, that, assuming at a particular time the danger threatened on only one coast, the minimum force adequate to maintain an effective naval patrol, to say nothing of engaging in any fighting, would be on one coast six torpedo-boat destroyers, four mine-sweepers and twelve auxiliary vessels. And it should be remembered that we have on the Pacific coast between 1,200 and 1,500 Japanese fishing vessels. We might as well face the fact that at the present time the only attack we need fear would come from Japan; and as I say, we have on that coast from 1,200 to 1,500 Japanese fishing vessels, some of which at least are manned by ex-naval men from the Japanese navy. One can imagine, therefore, what sort of protection we need there in the way of a mosquito fleet.
But the minister went on to point out other tasks of the navy. At page 3263 of Hansard he said:
The tasks of the navy 'are:
1.	In cooperation with the air force to reconnoitre coastal maritime regions, focal sea areas and their vicinities.
2.	In cooperation with the land and air forces to destroy surface craft and submarine raiders.
3.	To provide examination services at our main seaports.
4.	In cooperation with the land forces to provide anti-motor torpedo boat and antisubmarine protection for our main seaports.
5.	To keep the approaches to our main seaports clear of mines.
This would appear to call for more destroyers and motor torpedo-boats, a bigger mosquito fleet and possibly several submarines and even a cruiser; yet we are getting this year, notwithstanding the crisis we are facing, only one flotilla leader, and no one knows whether that is to be stationed at the naval station on the Pacific coast or on the Atlantic coast. In connection with the naval requirements of the dominion I would refer hon. members again this year to the recommendation made by Lord Jellicoe to the Canadian government after a thorough investigation in 1919, wherein he said:

Supply-National Defence
The naval force suggested as adequate purely for the protection of Canada's trade and Canada's ports under the conditions assumed comprises:
3 light cruisers,
1 flotilla leader,
12 torpedo craft,
8 submarines with 1 parent ship
and certain auxiliary small craft for training purposes, etc.
That was immediately after the war when conditions were not as menacing as they are at the present time. I suggest that Canada should proceed as quickly as possible to obtain her requirements in ships, and that in the meantime an attempt be made to secure help from Great Britain for the establishment of a proper North Pacific squadron. The minister pointed out that it was comparatively easy to get ships in an emergency, and I assume they would come from Great Britain.
But have we any plan for the Canadian navy? Are we building or buying according to a plan? So far the government have not announced any plan in any session of this parliament. The other day the minister announced an army plan and an air plan, but it is always hush-hush with reference to a naval plan. The people of Great Britain and Australia are told year after year precisely what their governments plan in the way of naval protection, but the Canadian people are given no information whatever.
I submit that we should know at what the government are aiming.
Furthermore, we should be building smaller craft in Canada now, such as the mosquito fleet to which I referred a few minutes ago. The other night the minister said that the government were proposing during the coming year to draw up complete working plans for the building in Canada of anti-submarine vessels, motor torpedo-boats and a training schooner. I suggest that the time has come to build such boats and not to spend the whole year in drawing plans. Why should there be this delay? In fact we should be building boats for Great Britain. Last October Doctor S. F. Dorey, chief engineer surveyor of Lloyds Registry, stated publicly in Vancouver, as reported in the Vancouver Province of October 28, 1938, that small craft of the British navy, mine-sweepers and sloops, might well be built in Vancouver. I suggest that the government ascertain what can be done along that line. It would mean the development of a shipbuilding industry in Canada and would provide that much more employment. So much for the navy.
I have also certain suggestions to make with respect to the militia. On the Pacific coast, which, as I have shown, is one of Canada's
two front lines, we have not a sufficient number of men to man the forts, and my authority for that statement is Colonel H. F. G. Letson, M.C., an officer with a distinguished record both in war and in peace, the honorary adviser for British Columbia to the militia department. In a public speech delivered in Vancouver in March, about two months ago, as reported in the Vancouver Province of March 6, 1939, he said:
I estimate that we have to-day in British Columbia less than one-third of the trained personnel that is required to man our fixed defences and maintain our internal security in time of war.
He is the officer actually in command of the 14th brigade of militia in the city of Vancouver. I suggest that the units in the two coastal areas should ibe brought up to strength at once, and if necessary the government should advertise for recruits. The minister declared the other night that the turn-over in the militia was discouraging. He said that men were joining and leaving. The same complaint has been made to me in Vancouver time and time again. I was told the same thing at Easter and that recruiting was falling off instead of increasing. If we are to be able to recruit men for the Canadian militia, we must make service in the militia more attractive. For example, at the present time I understand-the minister will correct me if I am wrong-that our militia men receive no pay for the time they spend in training in their barracks. There is certain pay during the time they are at camp, but no pay during the winter when they are being trained in the barracks. No provision is made for carfare going to and from the barracks. I believe that Canada has the only volunteer force in the world that is not paid for undergoing training of that kind. You cannot expect men to join the militia and give up their time if they are not treated more reasonably. With regard to the clothing, last fall I heard of one unit in Vancouver which expected to get new clothing, and after waiting for months and months, they got uniforms made during the war, in the United States of America. That sort of thing is not good enough.
Then I suggest that there should be a regular permanent force adjutant or permanent force orderly room sergeant attached to each large unit. I believe that is the practice followed in the territorial army in Great Britain. There should also, of course, be a proper supply of equipment. Apparently the minister was at a dinner in Ottawa on March 21 of the Dominion of Canada Rifle Association; and I find in a report in the Ottawa Journal of March 22, 1939, the following:
Supply-National Defence

Captain H. J. Bowen of Ottawa declared that the falling off of interest in rifle shooting was due to the fact that many of the rifles issued to the militia wrere no longer serviceable. He knew of one case where out of 40 rifles issued only 8 could shoot anywhere near the target.
And I get similar reports from Vancouver.
I was not present at the dinner, but I was present there in the morning.

Well, I think the statement is correct anyway.
My next suggestion has to do with highways. At present there is no highway across the province of British Columbia; the trans-Canada highway will not be completed until next spring. Canada should maintain at least one first class military highway from Alberta to the coast, and eventually should also have such highways through to Prince Rupert and probably Stewart as well as one through the southern part of the province; first class military highways. They would, as the minister knows, be invaluable for defence purposes. For this purpose why can we not expand our Royal Canadian Engineers of the permanent force? Let them take charge of these military highways. The same idea could be adopted in the other parts of Canada where it is necessary to make arrangements for defence. In British Columbia many of our first roads were built by Royal Engineers who came out from Great Britain, and some of the roads are still in use.
Then, with regard to our forts and gun installations, this government during the last few years have spent millions on fortifications on the Pacific coast. I suggest to the minister that there should be a committee of members of parliament representative of all parties, entirely non-political in its set-up, to go over and investigate these fortifications. That is done in Great Britain. I have here a clipping from the Ottawa Journal of March 11, containing a picture of British members of parliament at Aldershot. The heading is:
British M.P's taken into army's confidence.
The article below goes on to say:
Mr. Hore-Belisha, the Minister of War, was not there himself-there was a cabinet meeting -but he had commanded a showing of the army s closest secrets, and 148 M.P's ploughed through Aldershot's yellow mud to see them.
I may say to my hon. friend that we shall be only too glad at any time to arrange for any member of parliament to go and see any of these fortifications.

It is not a matter of one member of parliament going to see them, it is a matter of a committee of this house going. 
I was long enough in the army to know that regular army men are not infallible, neither are army contractors; and a little common sense mixed in with army administration goes a long way, as the Canadian corps showed in the great war. I suggest it is absolutely unsound that we should be sitting here voting money for these fortifications and relying on- the minister alone; I suppose no other member of parliament has the slightest idea of what is going on, how this money is being spent, and whether we are getting efficient work. There are rumours on the Pacific coast about defective work. For example, there are the Stanley park guns. I asked the minister last year on May 16 about the two guns in Stanley park, when the installation would be completed, and he assured me it would be completed in June, 1938. This year on February 22 I asked again the same question. The question was:
1.	Have the fortifications in Stanley park, Vancouver, been completed and turned over to the Department of National Defence?
2.	If so, on what date were they turned over?
And the answer was that the works were not yet completed, and it was expected that they would be turned over by the end of June, 1939.
The guns were installed some time ago.

In other words, a year late. And apparently there was trouble with flooding; the guns were set on a spring, or it may have been just our Vancouver rain; at any rate there was trouble with flooding of the emplacements; the emplacements were not properly wired, and the guns cannot be fired; all pointing to the necessity for some check on these fortifications.
Then there is the question of equipment and munitions, more important now than ever before, and calling for more advanced training of troops. Yet we find from the minister's speech as reported at page 3256 of Hansard a list of equipment that Canada needs and cannot get. As the minister put it, his officers had told him that these were the proper weapons and stores of ammunition to put the militia service in a position to discharge with reasonable efficiency its share of the duty of national defence for Canada. In other words these are the materials required before the militia can function. Here is the list:
Coast Defence Armament for both East and West Coasts-
12 heavy coast defence guns 9 mountings for heavy guns 4 medium guns 3 mountings for medium guns 6 light quick firing guns

Supply-National Defence
Anti-Aircraft Armament-
123 anti-aircraft guns with equipment of four different types
Mobile Army Requirements

544 infantry mortars 60 medium howitzer equipments 20 medium gun equipments 500 field gun equipments 348 anti-tank equipments
Together with the necessary ammunition. He went on to say that we simply could not procure those supplies, that England could not spare them. Apparently the government's policy is to wring their hands and wait. Meanwhile our citizen soldiers are expected to fight with their bare hands and apparently, to date at any rate, to fight our battles in their own boots.
In my opinion there is not enough equipment in Canada to equip fully the Vancouver brigade alone, let alone the whole militia of Canada. For example, what are we to do about rifles? We have had practically none here since the war, I believe, except the rifles brought back with us from France. On March 14 of this year I asked the minister the government's policy with regard to rifles, were they to be purchased or manufactured? His answer, found on page 1896 of Hansard, was:
The government's policy in that regard will be determined in the future. At the moment I am not in a position to state definitely what it will be.
1 suggest that the government adopt a policy of extending the dominion arsenals so that they can manufacture at least a portion of all our requirements. Perhaps Great Britain would work with us in extending these arsenals; probably she would be only too glad to have some of her equipment turned out in them. The main link missing in the chain of defence Canada is preparing is the adequate extension of the dominion arsenals so that they can produce at least a portion of all types of equipment required. That is the policy followed by Great Britain and the United States. Australia, as a matter of fact, has gone much further in the public manufacture of armaments. The whole question was thoroughly investigated in England, as the minister knows, by a royal commission on the private manufacture of and trade in arms in 1935 and 1936. I should like to read one section from the recommendations of that commission. Incidentally, when the minister read this section some weeks ago, he left out a portion of it, which I think he should not have done. It may have been, a slip, but the whole paragraph should have been read; it is No. 6, and reads as follows:
We recommend that the government should assume complete responsibility for the arms industry in the United Kingdom and should organize and regulate the necessary collaboration between the government and private industry; that this responsibility should be exercised through a controlling body, presided over by a minister responsible to parliament, having executive powers in peace time and in war time, over all matters relating to the supply and manufacture of arms and munitions, costing and the authorization of orders from abroad.
Then we find this further small paragraph which the minister omitted:
We further recommend that the government's own manufacturing establishments should be fully equipped for the production in some measure of naval, military, and air armaments of all types.
Yet in Canada to-day, although we have two arsenals, one at Quebec and one at Lindsay, we are only manufacturing ammunition. We shall have to manufacture military equipment for an indefinite period, and I suggest that the sooner we get on a proper basis, with the government arsenals supplying at least a portion of all types of military equipment the sooner we shall be out of this difficulty.
My last suggestion is that an embargo should be placed on the shipment of war materials to aggressor nations, and particularly to Japan. A year or two ago we in Vancouver had the experience of seeing our small destroyer, named after the city, H.M.C.S. Vancouver, being broken up and the steel and scrap-iron placed on scows, eventually being sold to Japan, not directly by the government but by the contractors who bought the ship for junk. At the same time we saw Canada rushing her defences, obviously against Japan. These two things taken together do not make sense. There should be an embargo against the shipment of war materials to Japan, if for no other reason than that last September Japan was found by the League of Nations to be an aggressor nation, and Canada, as one of the family of nations, should see that such an embargo is imposed.
My hon. friend knows, of course, that the Vancouver was never owned by this government.
It was part of the Canadian navy.
On loan.
It was defending our Pacific coast and was scrapped and sent to Japan to be made into shells and other war material.

The
Canadian government had no financial interest in the Vancouver.

The Canadian government did all the managing of the ship.
Supply-National Defence
In what year did that occur?

My authority for the state-mnt that Canada should take action and place an embargo against war materials going to aggressor nations is no less a personage than our present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). On April 1, 1935, speaking before the last election, to an amendment moved by Mr. Bourassa reaffirming adherence to the treaty for the renunciation of war, the Prime Minister used words which I think were remarkable, in view of this government's refusal up to the present time to impose such an embargo. He said:
I think this country ought to declare that any nation which could be shown to have threatened the peace of the world by violating a pact of collective security should be denied any assistance in the shape of men or munitions, should be denied any assistance in the nature of food, should be denied any assistance through credit. Our country, small as it is, might well lay down a definite policy in that regard as expressing Canada's attitude toward any country which upon the facts being disclosed was found to be guilty of attempting to destroy what otherwise might be collective security. If that example were followed by other parts of the British empire, as I believe it would be, it would soon be followed by other parts of the world.
All one can say about that is that the Prime Minister was a great deal bolder in 1935 than he is in 1939.
In conclusion, may I say that for the first time in this twentieth century the Canadian people are forced to think of the possibility of there being invaders on Canadian soil. No longer isolated, we are being brought closer every day to potential enemies by the development of aircraft. And the Canadian people are now defence conscious, a people who can face an ugly situation with courage. But they should be told the facts. The government should tell them the whole story. Our defence policy should be a long-range policy on a permanent basis, not a rush here and then a rush back, with great excitement and great mystery, all of which upsets our people. We shall always have to defend ourselves, so we might as well get our defence forces, defence equipment, fortifications and other defence works on an efficient basis without further delay. The sooner we attain that position, the sooner we can stop worrying about the situation.
Finally I hope that in planning the defence of Canada this Canadian parliament and the Canadian people will not lose the vision of world peace, which, in my opinion, can be brought about only by some system of collective security, probably through a revitalized league of nations. These stormy days through

which we are passing will not last forever; and Canada, when the opportunity arises, should be right in the front rank of the nations trying to find the road to permanent world
peace.
Mr. LIGUORI LACOMBE (Laval-Two
Mountains) (Translation): Mr. Chairman, my attitude has not changed; I strongly object to any increase in defence appropriations. On several occasions I have set forth in this house the reasons which compel me to oppose this rearmament policy. I shall therefore confine my remarks to a reaffirmation of the principles which, in my humble opinion, should guide the government in its defence policy. Its first duty should be to amend the Militia and Naval Service Acts so as to bring them into conformity with the statute of Westminster. The existing Militia Act authorizes Canada's participation in external wars. It even contains a conscription clause which, in the event of war, would compel Canadians to participate willy-nilly in military activities not solely directed to the defence of Canadian territory. This act goes so far as to provide, in section 69, page 2790 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1927, as follows:
The Army Act for the time being in force in Great Britain, the King's Regulations, and all other laws applicable to His Majesty's troops in Canada and not inconsistent with this act or the regulations made hereunder, shall have force and effect as if they had been enacted by the parliament of Canada for the government of the militia,
And so on.
Therefore, I shall as in the past, refuse to vote a single item of the estimates of the Department of National Defence. National defence, if words still have a meaning, means the protection of our territorial integrity and of our direct interests. Otherwise, it only means voluntary or compulsory participation in British and external wars. It means imperial defence, rather than national defence. It is not a question of canadianism but of imperialism. It is against that imperialistic sentiment that, as a Canadian, I must fight. It is in the name of the statute of Westminster, which was built on the ruins of the colonial status, that I still ask for necessary amendments to our Militia and Naval Service Acts, in order to ensure the exercise of the sovereign rights of our country, the protection instead of the ruin of our people, the respect for and full application of our constitution.
One more word. Let us proclaim immediately our neutrality, before it is too late. Otherwise, considering our present Militia and Naval Service Acts, I have good reason to

Supply-National Defence
fear that, one day, our country will be unjustly sacrificed on the altar of military and financial imperialism.
Referring to the speech of the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Francceur), may I remind the committee that we fought military appropriations from conviction and as a matter of principle. Moved by a truly Canadian spirit and solely by a sense of my duty to the country, I have adopted an exclusively Canadian attitude. In spite of the arguments advanced by the hon. member for Lotbiniere, I remain irrevocably opposed to the policy of the government concerning military matters. However, I would ask the hon. member not to ascribe to me motives at variance with the statements I have made in this chamber. My hon. friend will have to consult with the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) who claims that Canadian neutrality is an impossibility, before saying that we must arm in order to protect our neutrality.
In conclusion, I may say that, in order to affirm the entity and the identity of a great country, equal in status with any other nation of the British commonwealth, a Canadian flag should float high in the magnificent setting which will greet to-morrow the arrival of our sovereigns on our soil. Such a national emblem is needed more than ever in these difficult times. In that symbol, I already see the truly Canadian aspirations of a great nation and a great country.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few general remarks in connection with the defence of Canada, which is a matter of increasingly grave and great importance to those of us who live in this dominion, and to the British family of empire.
I have listened with great interest to the speeches of the minister and other hon. members who have spoken on this subject this session. One may have sympathy with that expression of opinion which ventilates a loathing of war, a loathing of the thought of the use of force. But those of us in this country who loathe war loathe it no more than do those who live in other peace-loving countries. To be compelled by circumstances to take up arms is no more repugnant to any of us in Canada than it is to anyone else who loves peace.
We cannot listen to speeches such as that made by the minister the other day in introducing these estimates without realizing immediately that we are in a strange position, in the midst of strange days. We are compelled to a realization that the world is in a state of flux, that we are passing through
desperate times and that we ourselves in this dominion have failed to take steps adequate to that position.
As citizens of a free country, enjoying liberty and freedom under a democracy, we are compelled to view with grievous concern the events of recent months and years, with the whole of our western civilization in a chaotic state, as a result of the conduct of an unspeakable few. There are those who loathe war just as much as does the hon. member who has just spoken, and who feel that any means we may take to avoid war are justified. But when force is developed to a staggering degree and this force used to promote bestiality and barbarism, and when that force grows and grows, insensible to any appeal to reason or humanity, what can be the answer but that force must be met either by a show of force or by force itself? And thus, Mr. Chairman, if we would maintain the peace of the world, and do our part to maintain that peace, are we not compelled to do our share to help develop that show of force which will be sufficiently impressive to resist the force which has been developed on the side of aggression.
In his remarks the other day the minister, by such a citation of figures as those he placed upon Hansard, demonstrated to us that our defence forces in Canada have been permitted to sink, may I say, essentially to an all-time low. He did not tell the committee, however-and I think he might have done as much as that-that the spirit of those days in which our militia and other forces were permitted to sink to that level, was a spirit of disarmament rather than armament. In common with Great Britain, the United States and other countries we were endeavouring to live up to the spirit of the times, and to pacts such as the Kellogg-Briand pact. Those were days, yes, of disarmament, rather than armament.
And then times began to change. An unsettled world gave birth to a Hitler. An unsettled world gave a chance to such a man to rise to unprecedented power. Only a few years ago a new armament race got under way. There is not an hon. member in the committee but knows that so far as we in Canada are concerned we must rely upon our own forces to defend our own country. It may be glorious for us to proclaim that so long as the British navy is afloat we are protected. But if we assume such a cushy and soft attitude of complete reliance upon the mother country we must realize that our assumption in days such as these is without foundation. Let us face the facts. We are
Supply-National Defence

forced to the conclusion that the mother country has her hands more than full to defend her own shores and her own people.
Let me illustrate. I think I am safe in saying there never has been a time in recent Canadian history when our permanent force and our non-permanent militia have been so destitute of equipment. And why? We have passed substantial sums-some of us have felt they are not nearly adequate-in the past two sessions of this parliament, sums amounting to nearly $70,000,000. The minister in his remarks the other day reminded us that orders for modem equipment had been placed in the United Kingdom. But these orders have been placed where there has been going forward a furious and hectic race against time, a race conducted in the manufacture of armaments to resist an aggressor who at any moment might have struck or who might strike, with the result that there has been none left over for us, and accordingly our orders have remained unfilled. This position has been apparent to us in this house. It must also have been apparent to the government and to the minister in particular; but in the meantime, even though that position was so readily apparent, have we taken steps in Canada to rectify it?
We know fully well that in recent years the British territorial army has been increased enormously, and that in recent weeks under conscription hundreds of thousands of men are being called up. What chance is there of British manufacturers of arms being free to furnish us in Canada with our requirements? True, we are ready to pay for them, but the supply is limited. England needs all the armaments that she can produce.
It is staggering to some of us who sense the danger we are in, consequent upon our complete lack of preparedness to defend ourselves as a result of our hopelessly inadequate equipment here at home, that so little is being put forward to rectify this disgraceful position. And here we are, still juggling with our very national security. True, a survey has been made, so the minister tells us, of upwards of-is it 2,000 manufacturing plants-but with what results? I do not for a moment criticize this survey; in fact, I commend the minister for it. But if the survey is on paper in the Department of National Defence, and has been on paper and remains on paper, what immediate use is it to us while it remains on file?
The hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) in his remarks to-night drew attention to the fact that such arsenal equipment as we may have at the moment in buildings

at Lindsay and such other places is being used only in a mediocre and partial way. We have only to look to Australia to realize what the Australian has done to develop an arms industry to produce equipment to defend himself. There he has developed his pilot plants and has cooperated with industry from these pilot plants even to a fuller degree than has the United Kingdom herself. We have these plants, or what could easily be made irfto pilot plants, but we have taken no steps towards developing them as such. And here in the Department of National Defence remains this list of two thousand plants that have been surveyed, and as yet no steps taken, so far as the minister was able to tell us the other day, towards the practical operation of these plants in the production of our own military requirements.
We as a nation are ready and willing to resist invasion and to do our share to protect our heritage at home and abroad. But have we in Canada anti-aircraft guns to withstand attack from the air? There were three or four such guns ordered by the late government, and I believe eighteen guns have been ordered since, a few of which have been delivered. But surely we must realize, with the length of our shores both east and west, and with such a situation prevailing as has been drawn to the attention of this house over and over again with relation to Hudson bay and James bay, that we have no adequate protection? Have we fighting planes and bombers for the defence of our highly vulnerable points? Are the harbours of Vancouver, Halifax and Saint John equipped with adequate coastal defence? And what equipment have our infantry, artillery and other forces?
It may be readily understood, Mr. Chairman, as a result of the desire to disarm that possessed even the mother country in the days to which the minister referred, why we joined the parade and did not build up our defences. But that was years ago. Times have so completely changed that it is fatuous to compare 1939 with 1933 or 1934; for all of us who have taken an interest in what goes forward in Europe-and who is not compelled to take an interest in what goes forward in Europe these days?-know that the whole picture is completely different to-day from what it was then,
I speak to-night as a citizen of this country and as the father of a family. As surely as I speak, it is not an unfair question, and cannot possibly be construed as a political question, to ask the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) what have we done in recent years to develop our defence forces and to maintain

Supply-National Defence
our national structure against possible attack. Over $60,000,000, yes, nearly $70,000,000, have been voted in the last two years-and with what result? This year the minister asks for an equal amount, some $63,000,000. Surely this house and this committee are entitled to know what his plans are. How is he going to develop the armament manufacturing industry in Canada? Is it to be controlled by the state or is it to be controlled by private capital? What are his plans to produce military aircraft? What are his plans to train pilots? We heard the minister the other day say that some fifty pilots are to come from Great Britain to be trained here. Here is Great Britain engaged in the production of hundreds of aircraft a week, several hundreds, running almost into thousands a month, and pilots to fly these planes being trained in the most vulnerable area, the United Kingdom, when we could be contributing so much towards that end. Surely, Mr. Chairman, it is not taking the part of the aggressor if we share with the United Kingdom in her effort to protect herself, which is virtually our own protection.
As I said the other day in speaking on another subject altogether, it is difficult for us to contemplate what might happen to this dominion if Great Britain herself, as the mother country, were destroyed. It is inconceivable for us to consider what our Canada might be in the event of such an extreme catastrophe as that. Surely we are prepared, if in no other way, at least to assist in the training of those who will fly the planes of the United Kingdom. We have vast areas here, certainly more secure from attack than the fields of the United Kingdom, and while we are training fifty pilots, it is true, fifty are but a drop in the bucket. So we in this chamber have the right to know the plans of the minister to assist us further, and to assist the mother country, when we can do so much to help her in her race against time to develop an armed force of sufficient strength to enable her to say "no" to the aggressor who would destroy those things which we hold most sacred and real, and in her effort to protect the little fellow.
I do not believe there is a man in this house but must recognize, if he faces the facts, that, confronted with the present ghastly situation in Europe, we cannot afford longer to sit back in smug complacency and play about with this problem of defence. If there is any matter of the moment which is above party politics it is this question. Accordingly I urge the minister, with all the earnestness of which I am capable, to recognize the inevitable situation, namely, that the armaments manufacturers of Great Britain cannot fill our orders and that we at once are compelled to take steps to develop that industry in Canada. Why should not our Canadian workmen, so many thousands of whom are unemployed, receive the benefit of such developments? Why can we not manufacture here not only for ourselves but for the fulfilment of orders for the mother country, and even from the United States if she cares to place her orders with us?
May I say in conclusion that it may be all very well to refer to the circumstances of other years, but this is 1939, and the threat of war hangs over us. I am confident that Canadian industry and Canadian workmen stand ready, awaiting the leadership of the Canadian government, to bring into being, with the efficiency and dispatch characteristic of Canadians, facilities to manufacture in this country our vitally necessary defence requirements and to assist the mother country in her efforts to become so strong that her words shall once again carry the weight of authority, thus, in our own way, contributing to the maintenance of the peace we all love.
Mr. CHARLES E. FERLAND (Joliette-
L'Assomption-Montcatm) (Translation): Mr. Chairman. I have received from the county I represent several petitions in which my electors declare themselves totally opposed to participation in foreign wars and to any joint action with London concerning European affairs, because claiming to be free from all outdated colonial spirit, they state their sons are ready to shed their blood only for the defence of their own country.
I have one of these petitions before me; the others were sent to the Prime Minister's office. This one comes from St. Jacques l'Achigan and carries about ten signatures. Attached to it is a second one entitled "Petition against conscription" and consisting of about ten pages covered with signatures. It seems therefore that my electors are in fear of two things, first, that Canada might take part in foreign wars, and, second, that such participation might eventually bring this country once more to adopt conscription. It is to the credit of my electors that, while admitting the necessity of providing for national defence, they say their sons are ready to shed their blood only for the defence of their own country.
Hear, hear.

Personally, I have always been, and will always be, opposed to the country's participation in foreign wars.
There is no doubt that all the agitation stirred up lately in the country, all the con-
Supply-National Defence

flicting statements that were made, all the curtailed and misquoted speeches of our leading statesmen which were published, have created a lot of confusion in the minds of Canadians, particularly among my compatriots.
May I be allowed to refer briefly to some important statements made by distinguished leaders of the Liberal party? First of all, at the beginning of the session, the Prime Minister made a statement which was misinterpreted, having been both wrongly and incompletely quoted. Recalling the policy of Sir Wilfrid Laurier in regard to England's wars, the Prime Minister quoted the doctrine of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, as follows:
If England is at war we are at war and liable to attack. I do not say that we shall always be attacked, neither do I say that we would take part in all the wars of England. That is a matter that must be guided by circumstances, upon which the Canadian parliament will have to pronounce and will have to decide in its own best judgment.
Only a part of this statement was published and it was said throughout the country, and particularly in the province of Quebec, that the doctrine of Sir Wilfrid Laurier was as follows: When England is at war, Canada is at war and must take part in all wars. That was the wrong interpretation which caused so much confusion. To say that Canada is liable to attack when England is at war is altogether different from saying that Canada must take part in all England's wars. At different times, the Prime Minister fully stated Canada's position in the British empire and as regards our relations with other countries. Has he not stated on several occasions, before the League of Nations and even in London, and time and time again on the floor of -the house, that Canada had now become a sovereign and independent state and was under no obligation to take part in any war outside its borders? Has he not stated time and time again what position parliament should take, from a truly Canadian point of view, in the event of war? Well do I know the existence of another school of thought in this country! It is the school of out and out imperialists, a school which proclaims -that should England be once more involved in war, Canada would again raise an army of
500,000	men, Canada would conscript both men and wealth, and Canada would contribute her last dollar and send her last son to England for the defence of the mother country or of the empire. But, Mr. Speaker, such is not the policy of the Liberal party, the policy of my leaders, far from it. Our leaders tell us repeatedly and have constantly stated, for the last year or two, that the military appropriations are solely intended to serve for the defence of Canada and that they are not to
[Mr. Ferland.l
be used in preparation for Canadian participation in the wars of Great Britain and the empire nor in any wars abroad.
Let us refer to what our leaders have stated on these two main points concerning which an attempt is made to create confusion in the minds of my fellow countrymen. Let us take conscription first of all. Here is what the right hon. Prime Minister, speaking in the House of Commons on March 30, 1939, said:
The present government believes that conscription of men for overseas service would not be a necessary or an effective step. Let me say that so long as this government may be in power, no such measure will be enacted.
And the great political leader making this statement is the same man who, side by side with Sir Wilfrid Laurier, fought conscription during the great war and then went down to honourable defeat in his North York riding.
Hear, hear.

Listen now to another right honourable member of this house, our distinguished fellow-citizen of whom we have always been so proud, the right hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe):
I think I am true to my concept of Canadian unity when I say that I shall always fight against this policy; I would not be a member of a government that would enact it; and not only that, but I say with all my responsibility to the people of Canada that I would oppose any government that would enforce it.
Such sentiments are truly Canadian, Mr. Chairman. Such statements come from sincere men who have remained long enough in the public service, and who have discharged their duty and responsibilities toward the nation in such a manner that no one, particularly among our fellow-citizens, has any right to doubt their -word. Some will say: We question your statements and do not know whether you are sincere and whether you are telling the truth. Well, for my part,
I am satisfied that the words of our leaders in Ottawa, the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice or the other ministers who have made statements to the same effect, are as good as their bond. However, the same was not always true with the Conservative party. Was the word of their leader as good as his bond? How could he so quickly change his mind, when he violated the promise made during the war to the effect that there would be no conscription?
What is the present stand of our leaders on the question of Canadian participation in external wars? The Prime Minister said, in this chamber, on March 30, 1939:
One strategic fact is clear: the days of great expeditionary forces of infantry crossing the

Supply-National Defence
oceans are not likely to recur. Two years ago,
I expressed in this house the view that it was extremely doubtful if any of the British dominions would ever send another expeditionary force to Europe. . . .
We have tremendous tasks to do at home, in housing the people, in caring for the aged and helpless, in relieving drought and unemployment, in building roads, in meeting our heavy burden of debt, in making provision for Canada's defence, and in bringing our standards of living and civilization to the levels our knowledge now makes possible. There is no great margin of realizable wealth for this purpose; we must, to a greater or less extent, choose between keeping our own house in order, and trying to save Europe and Asia.
The Minister of Justice said, for his part:
I agree with what was said yesterday by the leader of the opposition and the Prime Minister, and what was said by Mr. Bruce of Australia, that the time for expeditionary forces overseas is certainly past, and it would not be the most effective way to help our allies. The men would be needed here; and in any event it is parliament which will decide about it.
Those words, also, should be satisfactory to the people of the province of Quebec, a people which in the past has shown that it had an enduring faith and a growing respect for the leaders of the Liberal party, for the Prime Minister and for the members of his cabinet.
Another question has to be considered concerning the increase in the defence appropriations. We should examine if these appropriations are justified by the circumstances of the hour. We are agreed on the necessity of defending our territory and I reaffirm that principle. It remains to be decided to what extent we should organize our defence. That is a technical problem about which I have not much knowledge, although I claim to possess as general a knowledge of things as most hon. members. Is Canada in danger of being attacked?
The leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) discussed that question this afternoon, and here are the principles he laid down as to the possible dangers of attack upon Canada and the need of preparing our national defence.
In the first place, Canada is not only threatened but is without adequate defences. The leader of the opposition, consequently, is of the opinion that the military appropriations are insufficient.
In the second place, he said that the government is neglecting the defence of the country or is not sufficiently hurrying our armaments.
In the third place, even in the absence of any immediate danger of war, it is necessary to prepare the defence of Canada in order to ensure her neutrality in the event of war
with Japan and the United States. He does not say in the case of war between Japan and England, because he expressed the opinion a few days ago that Canada cannot remain neutral when England is at war because, according to him, the British crown is indivisible and the King cannot be at war in respect of one of his dominions or one part of the empire and be neutral in respect of another part. Finally, the leader of the opposition added this:	"I suggest an increase of defence
appropriations as a means of relieving unemployment."
I shall quote another Conservative member because he comes from my province and has in his constituency a large number of Frenchspeaking electors and a certain number of English-speaking ones. I refer to the hon. member for Argenteuil (Mr. Heon). Speaking in this house on January 30 last, he began by vaguely criticizing the present government's defence policy, but afterwards left a wide opening for those of his constituents who are in favour of the defence of Canada by saying:
I want to make it clear before I terminate my remarks that I am not a pacifist in the narrow sense of the word. I believe it is our strict duty to make this component part of the commonwealth invulnerable to attacks and invasion. If this government has been reliably informed that some foreign power has cast a covetous eye on this territory, and if this information originates from authoritative and unimpeachable sources, then it is our immediate and sacred duty to proceed with the speediest, most complete and most efficient plan for the defence of our homeland. I do not infer that we should never take part in any war. What I say is that any war in which we do take part must be a war in which something better than sentiment actuated by prejudiced propaganda is at stake. It must be a war that threatens our very liberty, independence and existence, and the issue of which would be of immediate vital concern to all of us.
Is that not the doctrine preached by the Liberal party, Mr. Chairman? Has not the Prime Minister always said that Canada would never go to war unless her institutions were threatened and the liberty of her citizens endangered?
I continue. Is Canada in danger? Here is the answer given by the Prime Minister in the House of Commons on May 24, 1938:
At present, danger of attack upon Canada is minor in degree and secondhand in origin.
Only part of this statement was quoted to-day during the discussion. It is important to quote the remainder:
It is against chance shots that we need immediately to defend ourselves. What may develop no one can say.

What is the opinion of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie)? Speaking also in this house on March 24 last, he said:
Now, sir, in regard to the scale of attacks upon Canadian territory or Canadian ports or terminals, these are considered by the experts who are supposed to be qualified to offer advice to be, in the first place, minor attacks by combined sea, land and air forces, to destroy something of strategic or commercial value, or to secure an advanced base of operations, and this applies to coasts, to focal sea areas and to the preservation of Canadian neutrality; in the second place, sporadic hit and run raids by light cruisers or submarines to destroy our main ports and focal sea areas.
In order to repulse such minor attacks and isolated raids, Canada is providing for the defence of her coasts, both east and west.
Our Conservative friends are forever repeating and proclaiming the necessity of preparing the defence of Canada. They are not satisfied with what the Liberal party has done; they even contend that Canada's defence is not sufficiently advanced. To hear them speak, one would think that Canada had no defences whatever. Their speeches would lead people to believe that in spite of all the millions voted for defence purposes nothing has been done, that we have no militia, no defence, and that we are more than ever exposed to external attacks. I therefore took the time to make a list of the elements composing our national defence.
Canada has a regular army of 4,201 men of all ranks, a non-permanent active militia (which is really the militia) whose peace strength amounts to 86,500, but whose present strength is estimated at about 49,000 men, plus, on paper, a reserve militia.
Her naval power consists of 6 destroyers, four of which are stationed in the Pacific. Two of these ships were built in England for Canada in 1930. The other four were built for the Royal Navy in 1932; Canada also owns five mine-sweepers. The present strength of the Royal Canadian Navy is set officially at 137 officers and 1,582 ratings, plus a volunteer reserve, corresponding to the non-permanent active militia, of 123 officers and 1,344 ratings, and a naval reserve of 70 officers and 430 ratings. The air force consisted, at December 1, 1938, of 249 permanent officers and 1,827 men of various ratings, and of 87 officers and 791 men (non-permanent). On December 1, 1938, the air force had 217 aircraft in active service. The authorized number of permanent squadrons is set at 10, and that of non-permanent squadrons at 12. The establishing, throughout the country, of landing 
fields, parallel to the development of Trans-Canada Airways, makes possible a rapid concentration.
Let us now examine our expenditures, in connection with national defence, during the last three years. Firstly, our Canadian militia cost us, until 1935, about twenty millions a year. In a report tabled in the house by the hon. Minister of National Defence on May 10, 1939, it appears that her national defence has cost Canada, during the last three years, the following amounts:

These figures therefore reveal, Mr. Chairman, that the honourable Minister of National Defence did not spend the entire amounts authorized by parliament and which he had at his disposal.
Since the defence of Canada must be organized in view of imminent dangers, and since, at present, there still remain threats of war on the horizon, and, moreover, seeing it is a fact that an attack was made on Canada during the great war by a German submarine which tried to assail fishing vessels in Canadian territorial waters and even sank a large ship at Halifax, it is important to establish that the government intend to increase or to reduce the militia or the military estimates according to circumstances or the needs of the moment. If it was possible, during the last three years, not to spend all the amounts authorized, it is to be hoped that, should the threats of war disappear, and I trust we shall not have a war, the government or the Minister of National Defence will not spend the entire defence appropriations but that they will find a way to reduce them as it became possible to do and was done during the last three years.
Now, before concluding, and in order that there may be no misunderstanding in the province of Quebec about the principles underlying the Liberal party's external policy,
I shall quote the basic principles which the Prime Minister himself laid down last year in this parliament:
These principles were as follows:
1.	The principle which must be followed in formulating Canada's external policy is the preservation of unity in Canada as a nation.
2.	The foreign policy of Canada, generally speaking, does not lie in her relations with the League of Nations but in her relations with the United Kingdom and the United States.
3.	Canada must, as a rule, keep in the background, in Geneva or elsewhere, whenever European or Asiatic interests are discussed.

4. Canada is in no way bound to adopt military sanctions imposed by the League of Nations, neither is she bound to defend any other member of the Commonwealth.
5. Canada is in no way bound to apply economic sanctions imposed by the League of Nations.
6.	In future, before accepting to participate in any military or economic sanctions, or in any war, the Canadian government will have to secure the approval of parliament or the Canadian people.
Such principles are truly Canadian, and they are quite different from those which have been expounded by the supporters of the utterly imperialistic doctrine that whenever England is at war Canada is at war. Of the two doctrines, I prefer the one expounded by my leader; I prefer the one to which my party adheres, and according to which the interests of Canada shall always come before every other consideration and nothing shall be done that is not germane to Canada's interests and is not wholly in behalf of Canada.
Mr, A. J. BROOKS (Royal): The debate this evening has, I am sure, been interesting to all of us, particularly on the question of defence. Canada's defence is becoming more and more the most vital concern of our people. This is as a result of the obvious and real danger to this country in the event of war, in which Great Britain or the empire might be involved, breaking out in Europe or any other part of the world. The impossibility of Canada remaining neutral was thoroughly discussed in this house some weeks ago in the debate on external affairs. Anyone in Canada giving this matter even the minimum of serious thought would agree with the expressions that were uttered at that time by leading members of the cabinet, and more particularly the opinion expressed by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion). I should like to quote what our leader said at that time, which I think is appropriate:
I feel-and I think it is the feeling of most Canadians who have given thought to this subject-that we cannot be in and out of the empire at the same time. It seems to me that it would be just as impossible for us to be neutral in a war in which Great Britain participated as it would be for my right arm to be defending my body against an assailant wishing to take my life, while my left arm remained friendly with the assailant. It seems very clear, to me at any rate, that that is just as logical as would be the idea of neutrality for Canada while remaining in the empire. We cannot be neutral and at the same time remain part of a great empire. . . .
I believe those words express the feeling and the sentiment of every true Canadian. The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie), in a long and interesting speech

on April 26, outlined some of the plans for strengthening our defences. He called attention to the fact that there was no need of defence on the south. This, of course, is a self-evident fact; as the leader of the opposition said this afternoon, a war with the United States would seem like a fratricidal war. The minister spoke of our north being icebound and said there was no necessity for defence in that direction. I should like to point out to the minister, however, that there is some danger in the north. He knows, as I do, that the most direct air routes leading into Canada come across the north from Labrador.
Our main defences are required on the east and west, on the Atlantic and on the Pacific. The minister's conclusions in this connection are quite clear. If Canada is attacked in either a major or a minor way, it must be on either the Atlantic or the Pacific coast. This evening I listened with pleasure to the address of the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green), who clearly outlined the position on the Pacific coast and touched on many other points in connection with Canada's defence. Coming from the maritime provinces I have felt that the necessity of defending our western coast has been stressed perhaps a little more than it should, to the disadvantage of the Atlantic coast. The minister is aware that there is only one potential enemy on the western coast of Canada, namely, Japan. For the last few years Japan has been engaged in a war with China, and I think it is quite understood that she has about all she can handle in that connection. So I say this idea of the western coast needing attention first, in preference to the Atlantic coast, has been over-stressed by the minister. I am not saying the western coast should be neglected, but I contend that fortifications on both western and eastern coasts should have been commenced and carried on at the same time. I sincerely believe that if there is any danger of an attack upon Canada we have more to fear in eastern Canada than in the west.
I might point out to the minister and to hon. members generally that during the great war, as was stated by the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare (Mr. Pottier) we had quite a number of submarines off the eastern coast. Only a few weeks ago there was a submarine reported off the southern coast of Nova Scotia. I recall that the minister denied the truth of this report, but nevertheless the rumour has persisted. Whether or not it was true, the fact remains that the people realized the possibility, and it did seem a serious matter at the time. The minister referred to the fact that in the past the British navy has been our defence, and went
